EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Wed, 14 Oct 2026 10:05:34 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.3 Listen: When does a hybrid attack become an attack on Nato? https://euobserver.com/242601/listen-when-does-a-hybrid-attack-become-an-attack-on-nato/ Wed, 14 Oct 2026 08:47:08 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242601 Two ships have been hit by drones in Bulgarian waters in the Black Sea on Monday. Several other ships have been targeted in recent weeks, at a time when Russia is intensifying its attacks on Ukraine.]]>

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

Find the full transcript below: 

Two ships have been hit by drones in Bulgarian waters in the Black Sea on Monday. Several other ships have been targeted in recent weeks, at a time when Russia is intensifying its attacks on Ukraine.

So, at what point does a hybrid attack become an attack on Nato? On Monday, two ships were hit by drones in the Bulgarian economic zone in the Black Sea.

One of them sank, with 11 crew members missing. The second vessel, which belonged to Ukraine, was damaged but did not sink, and all 15 people on board were rescued.

Read more

Drone strikes on Black Sea cargo ships point to wider European arc of Russia hybrid threats

A week earlier, two other cargo ships had been attacked by drones in the same area, killing 10 people. And on 5 October, a Turkish cargo ship carrying grain was sunk by drones shortly after leaving Ukraine.

There is currently no evidence proving that Russia was behind these attacks, and Moscow has not claimed responsibility.

But that did not stop Bulgarian Prime Minister Roumen Radev from summoning Russia’s ambassador. Radev said that, while there was no conclusive evidence, the outcome of these attacks clearly benefited Russia more than anyone else.

Russia’s ambassador to Bulgaria, Eleonora Mitrofanova, said she had received no information from the Russian defence ministry about the attacks. She also suggested that they could have been provocations carried out by a third party.

And that uncertainty is important, because it makes it much harder for Nato countries to decide when an incident should be treated as an attack.

Read more

[Interview] ‘Putin understands only strength’: EU envoy in Kyiv urges stronger air defences and hybrid-war response

So how do Europeans cope with these attacks? We’ve already seen several Russian drones end up inside EU territory in recent months. And in some cases, they have been clearly identified.

Take the Russian drone that crashed on a residential building in the Romanian city of Galați in May and injured two people. Or the two drones found at Leipzig airport in Germany this summer, charged with explosives. They were all identified as Russian.

So far, however, the response has consisted mainly of diplomatic measures and political statements. Neither Bulgaria nor Germany has requested formal consultations under Article 4 of the Nato treaty.

Article 4 allows a Nato member to ask for consultations when it believes its territorial integrity, political independence or security is threatened.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Radev has spoken with Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte about the incidents, which are serious enough to be discussed at Nato level. But Bulgaria has not gone as far as triggering Article 4.

One reason is precisely the ambiguity surrounding all these drone attacks: who is controlling them, whether they were deliberately sent into EU territory, and whether they were jammed or diverted.

Read more

Divided EU cyber defence faces real-life Russian and Chinese threats

But if an attack were clearly attributed to Russia, how would Nato respond? That’s one of the questions currently being discussed within the alliance.

On Monday, Nato’s top military commander, US General Alexus Grynkewich, said he did not believe a conflict between Russia and Nato was imminent or inevitable.

But he also presented what Nato calls a “theory of victory”: a plan designed to ensure that the alliance could rapidly neutralise an enemy attacking one of its members.

The strategy rests on several pillars. One is establishing clear red lines that an adversary should not cross. Another is investing in new military technologies, with drones playing a central role. And the third is maintaining the ability and readiness to fight at short notice.

The idea is not only to be able to respond if a direct attack happens, but also to deter Russia from continuing what Nato describes as hybrid activities against its members.

]]> The ‘Transformative AI Strategy for Europe’ diagnoses the problem – but its solution is capitulation https://euobserver.com/242300/the-transformative-ai-strategy-for-europe-diagnoses-the-problem-but-its-solution-is-capitulation/ Wed, 14 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242300 Europe can only fully prepare for the AI transformation and maintain our sovereign control if the default action is to consider how can we use or create a European solution first, rather than capitulate to what Big Tech offers.]]> Last month, a coalition of economists, politicians and AI experts released a report entitled Transformative AI Strategy for Europe. It provides yet more disturbing analysis of Europe’s deep dependency on overseas providers of essential AI. The concept of ‘Transformational AI’ is clearly gaining currency among policy elites as are the dangers it represents.

Co-signatory of the report, ex vice president of the European Commission, Margaret Vestager rightly comments: “We cannot allow Europe to become a playground for foreign powers. Our citizens are already bearing the economic and social consequences of decisions taken elsewhere. AI will accelerate this development, transforming our personal lives and relations, learning and jobs at an unprecedented pace.” 

Unrelated to the report, European Central Bank chair Christine Lagarde has also said: “A withdrawal of access [to AI models], or a change in its terms, would … reach every ​sector at once … That is leverage of a kind no trade partner has ever ​held over Europe, and it could be used in any negotiation, on tariffs or on digital taxes, for example.”

This is going to be expensive

Yet the solutions proposed by this assembly of experts would exacerbate, not mitigate, the control over European economy and society currently wielded by a handful of ultra-dominant, mainly US-headquartered, corporations.

Two approaches are outlined by the signatories of the report. One is to invest and build European frontier models to compete and participate as equals in the transformation AI economy. This, however, is almost immediately written off as too costly and too high risk to undertake.

The second, strongly recommended route, suggests trading power and land for access to frontier models – Europe will fast-track Big Tech build out on European soil in exchange for “guaranteed” preferential access to their frontier models.

This is little more than capitulation to the dominance of that handful of mega corporations under the control of foreign regimes. It is ironically resonant, in times when we speak of frontier models, of Native Americans trading land for a few trinkets – and we know how well that worked out.

Naïve expectation

It is naïve in the extreme to expect to negotiate lasting privileged access to frontier models in return for power and land in Europe. For one thing – Big Tech already has this access. Europe has a weak hand if trying to extract conditions in return for inward investment to build capacity that it needs.

In addition, current behaviours suggest that corporations and nation states already appreciate and are leveraging the economic and political power that possession of leading frontier models confers. Export restrictions on latest models are already in place, as are mark-ups of 20-50 percent to run models within defined jurisdictional boundaries, like EU clouds. 

Recent news unwittingly confirmed that the largest AI developers already guard and retain their best models for themselves. To solve part of the Navier-Stokes equation, a notoriously unsolvable maths riddle, OpenAI used, “a tool only used within the company, as it is “significantly more capable” than the company’s most recent AI model release.”

This clearly illustrates that OpenAI, and surely others, are keeping the best models to use internally. It is therefore inconceivable that Europe, or anyone, will really be able to negotiate access to the true frontier – we would be paying more for a worse model. This is not how you get ahead.

Surrender is not an option

Europe needs sovereign capacity and models to benefit from, rather than become subject to, transformational AI. Europe does not have to accept the Big Tech narrative on what or where the frontier is. Deciding for ourselves how AI can and should be deployed to have the most beneficial impact and best support European values is within our control and is our responsibility.

Regulation gets a bad rap, but one reason we have regulation is to enforce the values we share as Europeans. We care about product safety, fairness, and personal freedom. We do not accept intellectual property theft at massive scale in the name of technological innovation.

We may never catch-up to the US or Chinese frontier Large Language Models, but perhaps we should not blindly accept this as the right race to run. Asking ourselves how can AI positively transform what we already value in Europe must be the first question: what do we really want AI for? Then, perhaps Europe can work on its own large but focused AI models to leapfrog and create AI transformation that matters to us and conforms to our ideals and values. 

First, stop digging!

Action is clearly needed, and urgently. But the first step cannot be to negotiate away our assets be they land, power, data or values as part of a surrender to the status quo ante bellum.

The saying goes that when you find yourself in a hole (as Europe most surely is) stop digging. That means, as of now, stop giving new workloads to overseas AI and cloud giants by default.

We already have European alternatives for the majority of cloud services, and for AI, there are both European and open weight models that run with European providers – why are we not using them? Where there are gaps, we can develop bespoke European solutions with European providers. This creates reliable demand for homegrown AI models and compute capacity. It allows sovereign models to train and improve on sovereign data. Crucially, it deprives oversees models from using our data, resources and energy to further cement their control and dominance.

Buy or build European

Nudging public procurement towards European players grows the market and creates reliable demand against which venture capital and corporate funds can invest.

Only by flipping the paradigm – so that the default action is to consider how can we use or create a European solution first – can we fully prepare for the AI transformation and maintain our sovereign control.

]]> Could Islamophobia one day become EU law? https://euobserver.com/242540/could-islamophobia-one-day-become-eu-law/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 18:00:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242540 An Islamophobic EU Parliament motion has showed that Europe's Muslims have reached an impossible crossroads - to integrate and forget their roots, or stay true to their traditions and risk being treated as a fifth column. ]]> If the day should ever come where Islamophobia gets concrete legal backing in Europe, it could be soon.

The European Parliament (EP) just voted to “condemn the strategies of Islamist entryism” and to develop ways to disrupt Muslim political movements in a resolution on 8 October.

Some 381 out of 720 MEPs worry Muslims are seeking to infiltrate democratic institutions, weaken European rule of law, gender equality, and what they deemed “European values”. 

And almost every one of the centre-right and rightwing MEPs in the house voted to surveil EU funding for anti-racism organisations, so as to ensure none of it gets into the hands of the Muslim Brotherhood.

The brotherhood is a transnational Muslim group founded in 1928 in Egypt, involved in religious revival, social welfare, and political activism.

But according to a French government memo from May 2025, as well as the EP resolution, it is guilty of “entryism”, to sabotage French democracy.

The EP resolution and French memo were dubbed “a political witch-hunt targeting racialised people – particularly Muslim, migrant and refugee communities” by academics and civil society, like the European Network Against Racism (ENAR).

Read more

Centre-right’s Muslim Brotherhood witch-hunt in EU Parliament risks criminalising everyday activism

The group called the EP motion “a stain” on the EU Parliament, belonging “within the tradition of discredited far-right conspiracy theories.”

ENAR is among those the EU has sought to defund, due to rightwing views that its work aligns with Islamist threats.

The Forum of European Muslim Youth and Student Organisations (FEMYSO), a pan-European anti-Islamophobic group, which also risks EU defunding, said it had faced “relentless targeting and demonisation.”

Young Muslims in Europe were being forced “to choose between their identity and their right to belong,” FEMYSO president Hiba Latreche told EUobserver.

And the EP “witch-hunt” resolution, which was drafted by the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP) group and authored by its French MEP, Céline Imart, comes at a bad time for this demographic. 

Read more

Von der Leyen’s party backs mapping ‘Islamist networks’ and scrapping key EU asylum protection

Advocacy group Collective Against Islamophobia in Europe (CCIE) recently looked at 876 incidents of anti-Muslim hatred in Europe in 2025.

Four out of five incidents targeted Muslim women, 41 percent of which involved discrimination or violence linked to their headscarves.

Disturbingly, the documented episodes “occur predominantly in public or institutional spaces, highlighting the persistence of forms of institutional racism.”

But seeing as the EU Commission’s own anti-Muslim hatred group has been inactive since 2024, the prevailing view in Brussels appears to be that rampant Islamophobia in the EU is less of a problem than the imputed influence of a nebulous Islamic movement from Egypt, which is better known for providing social care to deprived communities, than aiming to overthrow French president Emmanuel Macron.

The EP motion did not legally bind the European Commission to propose new anti-Muslim Brotherhood measures.

But it did enforce a stereotype of Muslims “as acting in a nefarious, dangerous, anti-democratic manner, until proven otherwise,” said Omran Shroufi, a political science researcher at the Free University of Brussels.

Read more

Europe’s dangerous art of anti-Muslim doublespeak

Rightwing EU politics is pushing young European Muslims into a lose-lose, or Catch 22 situation.

The notion of “entryism holds Muslims to an impossible standard, where non-participation in public life is a sign of disinterestedness, a lack of civic duty and the growth of parallel societies, whilst active engagement in civic life is treated with suspicion,” Shroufi told EUobserver.

The centre-right EPP group used to represent a moderate EU mainstream.

But now it had joined with open racists on Europe’s far right to be “effectively calling for an institutionalised form of discrimination, where Muslim communities need to prove their European and democratic values – whatever these are supposed to mean – before being allowed a seat at a table,” Shroufi said. 

]]> Low pay and stress forcing Europe’s care workers to quit jobs, unions warn https://euobserver.com/242562/low-pay-and-stress-forcing-europes-care-workers-to-quit-jobs-unions-warn/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 16:59:22 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242562 Almost half of workers helping families care for children, older people, and people with disabilities in Europe have considered quitting due to low pay and bad working conditions.]]> Almost half of workers helping families care for children, older people, and people with disabilities, who provide vital domestic support in Europe, have considered quitting due to low pay and bad working conditions, a labour-union report found on Tuesday (13 October).

The 2026 personal and household services (PHS) employment monitor drew on more than 8,000 responses from workers, service users, and employers in 36 countries.

Around one in four respondents worked between 35 and 40 hours per week.

Meanwhile, six in 10 workers reported work-related musculoskeletal disorders, including back pain and tendon inflammation.

One in four also said they had experienced or witnessed verbal abuse, while nearly 15 percent had experienced either sexual harassment, physical, and/or sexual violence.

Care poviders’ mental health is impacted, with around six out of 10 reporting sleeping issues.

But these same workers play “an essential role in providing a dignified life for everybody in our ageing European societies,” Oliver Roethig, regional secretary of UNI Europa said in a statement.

]]> Ukraine killing record number of Russian troops, as Putin resorts to using gangs to boost enlistment (Ukraine Battlefield update, day 1,692) https://euobserver.com/242547/ukraine-killing-record-number-of-russian-troops-as-putin-resorts-to-using-gangs-to-boost-enlistment-ukraine-battlefield-update-day-1692/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 15:47:16 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242547 Soaring Russian casualty rates and shrinking recruitment mean frontline units risk running out of men to hold or advance in Donbas, even as Ukraine keeps blowing up their supply trucks and fuel tankers.]]>
  • Russia is estimated to be recruiting 10 percent fewer soldiers this year than last, despite regions raising signing bonuses.
  • There is growing talk that criminal gangs have begun to take part in recruiting “volunteers”.
  • According to the Ukrainians, Russia is losing large numbers of soldiers, and October could be a record month.
  • Attacks on the land route to Crimea continue, reportedly prompting Russia to transport fuel in jerry cans in smaller vehicles.
  • Map of the day: Where Russia is advancing and where Ukraine is advancing
  • Videos of the day: Ukrainians hit a Russian radar; a man surfed on a Russian drone near Odesa; speculation spreads that Iran is supplying Russia with fuel.

    • Many Russians have left Russia in recent months. They feared the mobilisation that had been so widely discussed. Ukrainians said Russian president Vladimir Putin might resort to it after the September parliamentary elections. Many Russians fled to Armenia and Georgia, affecting rental prices in the capitals of these Caucasus states.

    So far, no mobilisation has taken place. Russia continues to rely on its existing system of voluntary — and, in some places, involuntary — recruitment of new soldiers in Russian regions.

    German economist Janis Kluge, who tracks regional data, wrote last week that Russia recruits around 1,000 new soldiers a day (30,000 a month). That is less than last year — down six percent in September and 10 percent over the year as a whole.

    Nor did it help that, by his estimate, the sum paid by regions as a signing bonus had risen from $16,000 (€14,000) to $22,000.

    In some places, recruitment is also beginning to move into the illegal sphere. Kluge wrote that local criminal gangs were now becoming involved in the system.

    He mentioned the case of a prosecutor in Nizhny Tagil, a city of 400,000 in the Urals. In September, he appealed to the budget committee of the local duma.

    He complained that signing bonuses for Russian soldiers were leading to an increase in crime in the city. He called for payments to agents who find volunteers willing to sign an army contract to be stopped.

    According to Kluge, the prosecutor complained that criminal elements had become involved in recruitment in the city. He said an agent received $4,500 for finding one person to sign a contract.

    Many turned to gangs to help them, with the assistance of corrupt police officers or military recruiters who are part of the scheme. “And this ‘persuasion’ may also involve violence, as another case from Sverdlovsk region shows: two criminals forced their victims to sign contracts and then seized their bonus payments,” Kluge wrote.

    In Nizhny Tagil, 580 new soldiers were recruited last year, compared with 330 this year. It is not known how many of them criminal gangs helped to “persuade” in exchange for payment. In any case, the city does not want to change its system of rewards for agents because, in the words of the deputy mayor, it helps “fulfil our tasks”.

    Overall, it is becoming increasingly difficult for Russia to supply enough manpower to the front. Moreover, it is currently losing large numbers of soldiers there, and October’s losses could even be record-breaking.

    Ukraine publishes daily figures for killed and wounded Russian soldiers. These figures cannot be verified and may be inflated, but the trend suggests that the situation is worsening for Russia.

    The table below also shows this. According to it, Russia lost around 46,000 soldiers in September — more than 1,500 a day — making it, according to Ukrainian data, the second-worst month since the start of the war. The figure was higher only in December 2024.

    This October is on course to become Russia’s worst month in this respect. By the 12th day of the month, Russia had been losing an average of 1,620 soldiers per day. If Ukraine maintains this pace, it will be a record.

    Number of Russian military casualties per month, according to Ukraine. Source: minfin.com.ua

    Naturally, the question is how much these figures can be trusted. However, the Unmanned Systems Forces, a unit commanded by Robert Brovdi, known as Magyar, also publish figures for killed and wounded Russian soldiers.

    The Ukrainian units under its command compete with one another over which can strike more Russian targets. They receive points based on this, which they can then use to buy more drones. Individual strikes should therefore be confirmed by video.

    Given this, the data published by the Unmanned Systems Forces can be considered credible. They too indicate that October could be a record month, although their data cover only one-third of Russia’s total losses.

    Number of Russian soldiers killed and wounded by SBS drones

    Record-high losses and less substantial numbers of newly recruited soldiers suggest that Russia may have difficulties replenishing its units and, consequently, advancing further in Donbas or elsewhere.

    Attacks on the land route to Crimea continue. Last week, French OSINT analyst Clément Molin published a table according to which the number of Russian lorries and trucks struck had reached a record 770. Several videos show that the number of attacks on vehicles heading to Crimea or to the front in southern Ukraine remains high. They are simply not discussed as much because this is no longer new.

    Ukraine also destroyed the Chonhar bridge, which connects Ukraine with the Crimean peninsula. Russia has used a pontoon bridge there instead. This video shows Russian cargo vehicles crossing the pontoon bridge.

    The commander of Ukraine’s 41st Pilum Unmanned Systems Regiment, part of the 1st Azov Corps, recently provided interesting information on this issue. In an interview with Radio NV, he confirmed that the number of medium-range strikes was not declining and was increasing in some areas.

    He said that the operational zone overseen by Ukraine extended from 30 to 300 km.

    According to him, Russia is trying to bring as much fuel as possible to the front. Soldiers need generators to charge equipment, power radios and drones, and keep warm.

    However, Ukrainian attacks on fuel tankers are reducing Russia’s ability to bring fuel to the front. According to the commander, in the Dobropillia direction, where his unit operates, Russia began transporting fuel in convoys this summer and switched to distributing it in passenger cars or small trucks, carrying the fuel in jerry cans.

    This does not, of course, apply to all directions. However, an ongoing stream of new videos also confirms the destruction of fuel tankers.

    Map of the day

    Russian president Vladimir Putin’s latest — though certainly not final — deadline for capturing Donbas is by the end of this year. As on 14 previous occasions, it will not be met.

    Unlike in previous years, however, it appears entirely possible that by the end of the year the territory of the free part of Donetsk region could be even larger than it is now. This is suggested by a map published by French OSINT analyst Clément Molin. It highlights areas where Ukraine is advancing and areas where Russia is pushing forward.

    As can be seen, Russian forces largely hold the initiative in the north of Kharkiv region and at one location in the south of Zaporizhzhia region.

    In the crucial Donetsk region, however, the situation is balanced; indeed, it could be said that Ukraine holds the initiative in more places. More specifically, it is clearing the northern area above Lyman and pushing further south towards Velyka Novosilka.

    Source: Clément Molin

    Videos of the day

    Ukraine’s 15th Reconnaissance Artillery Brigade published a video showing it striking a Russian 96L6 radar. This is a key component of the S-300 and S-400 air-defence systems.

    The radar can be seen moving and hiding in a tree line. Nevertheless, a Ukrainian drone struck it. It is unclear whether it was actually destroyed, as the accompanying text claims.

    A man near Odesa decided to surf on a downed Russian drone floating on the water off the coast. It hardly needs to be said that this is a fairly risky pastime. However, it indicates how at least some residents of Odesa view the daily Russian attacks.

    This could be a potentially rather interesting plot twist. The United States is at war with Iran, which has raised petrol and diesel prices at US filling stations. Donald Trump therefore agreed with Putin to import diesel from Russia. Russia itself, however, does not have enough diesel and has to import it.

    This video shows a tanker truck with Iranian registration plates in Russia. Some infer from this that Iran is importing diesel — or other fuels — into Russia, which then sends diesel to America, despite America being at war with Iran.

    However, it is too early to draw conclusions: we do not know what is in the truck or how many such Iranian tankers are heading to Russia. In any case, Russia is helping Iran in other ways.

    A Western official told Bloomberg that Russia was supplying Iran with missiles that it uses in the war against the US and Israel. It was also previously reported that Russia was helping Iran target US bases in the region.

    What are the losses:

    • By Tuesday (13 October), Russia had verifiably lost 24,192 pieces of heavy equipment (24,170 on Monday, 5 October). Of these, 19,155 (19,133) were destroyed by Ukraine, 1,002 (1,003) damaged, 1,194 (1,194) abandoned by their crews, and 2,841 (2,840) captured by the Ukrainian army. The total includes 4,453 (4,452) tanks, of which 3,358 (3,357) were destroyed in combat.
    • Ukraine lost 12,259 (12,238) pieces of equipment, of which 9,652 (9,633) were destroyed, 713 (711) damaged, 695 (695) abandoned and 1,199 (1,199) captured. The total includes 1,471 (1,466) tanks, of which 1,131 (1,126) were destroyed in combat.

    Note: Neither side regularly reports its dead or destroyed equipment. Ukraine publishes daily figures for Russian casualties and destroyed equipment, which cannot be independently verified.     This article is paid for by JA Europe.

    On 15 September, the European Commission proposed a Skills Portability Act, a regulation designed to make qualifications digital, comparable, and easier to recognise across borders. It forms part of the Fair Labour Mobility Package and must still be adopted by the European Parliament and the Council before any of its measures can take effect. 

    It is a welcome step. But it leaves open a question that deserves more attention in Brussels: what happens to the skills young people develop every day but their diplomas and CVs do not capture? 

    Communication, teamwork, critical thinking, adaptability and resilience shape how people work with others and keep learning throughout their careers. Employers say they need these skills. According to the Commission’s 2023 Flash Eurobarometer, 74 percent of small and medium-sized enterprises reported shortages affecting at least one job role. Meanwhile, Eurostat found that in 2024 only 56.4 percent of people aged 15–34 in the EU with medium or high educational attainment reported a high or very high match between their field of education and the requirements of their current or last main job. 

    These figures measure different things and should not be read as pointing to a single cause. Together, though, they show that having qualified people and having the right capabilities in the right place are not the same thing. Young people build those capabilities in classrooms, vocational training, volunteering, creative projects and first jobs. Yet they struggle to show them in a form that an employer, particularly one in another country, understands and trusts. 

    The stakes are not abstract. In 2025, 11 percent of Europeans aged 15–29 were neither in employment nor in education or training. Skills recognition cannot resolve that on its own, but stronger links between learning and work are part of the answer. 

    In effect, we are asking young Europeans to cross borders with incomplete passports. 

    This is where micro-credentials can make a difference if they are built with credibility in mind. JA Europe coordinates EMPASS (Employment Skills Pass), an Erasmus+ Forward-Looking Project co-funded by the European Union. It brings together education providers, industry partners and Junior Achievement organisations to develop and validate an employability micro-credential covering 11 employability skills, from communication and teamwork to resilience and critical thinking. 

    The micro-credential was designed to be piloted with 1,500 students in Greece, Romania and Spain. According to the project’s latest monitoring figures, 2,700 young people now hold an EmPass certificate. 

    Beyond the pilot, the EMPASS approach is already demonstrating potential for wider uptake. The methodology has informed implementation and exploration activities in other countries, including Ukraine and Lithuania, and has been incorporated into wider youth employability initiatives such as the Global Alliance for Youth mentoring programme. This suggests that employability micro-credentials can be integrated into different learning and workforce-development contexts while maintaining a common framework for skills recognition. 

    A micro-credential does not replace a diploma, and no single certificate can capture everything a person brings to a job. Its value lies in complementing formal qualifications with clearer, validated evidence of what someone can do. The aim should not be another certificate that employers overlook. 

    Europe does not need more initiatives that show promise but struggle to reach scale. It needs bridges: between education and employment, between national systems, and policy ambition and lived experience. That means asking practical questions. Can a young person show the same verified capabilities to employers in different countries? Can employers see what microcredential assesses and how it was validated? Can schools and universities build it into existing pathways without adding administrative burden? 

    The answers will decide whether skills portability becomes opportunity or remains a policy ambition. They are also the focus of From Skills to Opportunity, a JA Europe forum in Brussels on 14 October, bringing together policymakers, employers, educators and youth organisations, including speakers from the European Commission, the World Employment Confederation and the European Vocational Training Association. 

    As the Skills Portability Act moves through parliament and council, Europe has a chance to put employability skills into the conversation from the start: not only how qualifications are recognised, but how capabilities developed through formal, non-formal and experiential learning can carry meaning across borders. 

    Employability skills are not an abstract policy debate. They are part of the foundation for participation, mobility, and opportunity in Europe’s labour market. The task now is to ensure that every young person carries a passport that employers recognise, wherever their learning and career take them.

    In France, 80 percent of those affected received warnings, but only 61 percent could act. Just 22 percent of households have a disaster plan, compared with 47 percent in Germany and 60 percent in Austria. And overall, France’s social resilience has fallen six points since 2021.

    Greece faces a deeper crisis of preparedness and confidence.

    Only 55 percent of disaster-affected people received warnings, and just 39 percent of those warned could act. Only 12 percent believe their government is well prepared, while 70 percent say it does not care about them.

But will MEPs dare use those powers in a budget fight with governments?]]> Getting co-decision powers on the budget, finally enshrined in the Lisbon Treaty after more than a decade of inter-institutional battles, was one of the European Parliament’s big wins. 

    The challenge facing MEPs in the coming months is whether they are really going to use those powers on the 2028-34 budget. 

    The early signs are that they are spoiling for a fight. The Irish government’s compromise proposal tabled on Saturday (10 October) – an 8 percent cut worth €141bn to the European Commission’s spending plan – isn’t exactly butchery. 

    But it does display a startling lack of ambition, in particular on the raft of ‘own resources’ proposed by MEPs to make the budget process less vulnerable to member states wanting to reduce or at least freeze their annual contributions  

    This time round, MEPs have proposed a digital services levy, an online gambling levy, and a levy on crypto-asset capital gains.

    Put together the parliament reckons that these new taxes could bring an additional €30bn to the EU’s budget, on top of the €57.4bn that the EU commission believes can be raised from other levies, such as the emissions trading scheme and the carbon border levy.

    ]]>         Forged news of military conscripts in Kaliningrad had hallmarks of a Western counter-attack in Putin’s info wars https://euobserver.com/242265/forged-news-of-military-conscripts-in-kaliningrad-had-hallmarks-of-a-western-counter-attack-in-putins-info-wars/ Mon, 12 Oct 2026 14:45:35 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242265 Western spymasters may finally be testing Kremlin-style information tricks on Russian soil to rattle Putin’s war regime.]]> A lethal plume of toxic smoke was blowing towards us from a blaze at a battery manufacturing plant in Kaliningrad.

    Troops in the Russian exclave had been ordered to help put the fire out: untrained and under-equipped, they mutinied. Terrified civilians were thronging the borders.

    The Kremlin, oblivious to the unfolding humanitarian and environmental catastrophe, blamed the West for sabotage and incitement, and demanded a transit corridor across Lithuania.

    However, none of this actually happened.

    We (20 retired and serving officials, experts, and others) were in the safety and comfort of the Wargaming Lab at the ISM university in Vilnius, as guests of the Baltic International Security Centre (BISC).

    The crisis scenarios were hypothetical; the aim was to explore the dilemmas and trade-offs they created. (You are the Lithuanian government. Do you let the mutineers in? Or leave them to be massacred?)

    The games-master provided regular “injects” – new developments – such as ill-written social media posts from US president Donald Trump. He blamed the authorities in “Lithvastonia” for having started the fire in “Kaliningradia”.

    An amusing parody, we thought. A few hours later, the real US president published news of his deal with Russian president Vladimir Putin on sanctions-busting diesel imports, then blamed Ukraine for being invaded.

    Not so amusing, especially for our Ukrainian participant, a senior military commander there.

    As we were leaving (us to safety, him to danger), news broke that Russia is stepping up its assassination attempts in Europe, targeting defence industry bosses (and perhaps Polish politicians). Our scenarios seemed tame in comparison.

  • They looked like Russian “porcupines” and fought where the Kremlin considers Russian rear territory. They were protected by their own drone.
  • Drones also struck Yandex’s third data centre.
  • The battle for Dobropillia on a new type of map.

    • They looked like Russian “porcupines” and fought where the Kremlin considers Russian rear territory. They were protected by their own drone. Both the Russian and Ukrainian armies are continuing their efforts to return tanks and combat vehicles to the battlefield.

    Russia recently attacked near Dobropillia with tanks fitted with upgraded Arena-M active protection systems.

    The system itself proved effective, but was ultimately unable to withstand the flood of drones, and the attack ended in defeat and the destruction of the tanks deployed.

    Last week, we also wrote about a successful operation by Ukrainian tanks from the 475th Assault Regiment.

    And the same Ukrainian unit, also known as CODE 9.2, demonstrated a new use of heavy armoured equipment over the weekend.

    Compared with the first case, this one revealed an important detail about the operation of accompanying drones and, thanks to geolocation, can also be used to verify the accuracy of Russian maps.

    The battle took place in the Kharkiv region and involved a US-made Bradley combat vehicle as well as a tank. According to one source, it was an Abrams of Australian origin, although the appearance of its gun barrel does not suggest this.

    In a video released by the unit, the Bradley advances first towards Russian positions and begins laying down covering fire. The tank joins it later, firing directly at the target.

    While the Bradley’s turret has retained its mobility, the tank has effectively become an assault gun of the type known from the Second World War.

    Its turret does not appear to be capable of moving, and the crew must aim the entire tank at the target. This reduces the effectiveness and speed of firing, while increasing its chances of survival.

    A tank modified in this way is virtually indistinguishable from similar Russian adaptations. What distinguishes these attempts is, once again, the involvement of accompanying drones.

    Aside from the heavy Vampire, first seen at 1:30, this primarily includes an FPV drone which, at 1:58, neutralises in an aerial duel the same type of Russian weapon that had attempted to strike the tank.

    This is another example of how heavy equipment must be accompanied by drones at this stage of the war if it is to remain combat-capable.

    Despite air support, another drone strikes it at 2:16 — after another had narrowly missed earlier. The tank remained mobile and withdrew successfully.

    Beyond the operation itself, its location is also noteworthy: near the village of Anishchyne in the north-eastern part of the Kharkiv region, on the axis Russia calls the Velykyi Burluk direction.

    The Ukrainian Telegram account Petrenko, which also provided the map below, precisely identified the site of the battle.

    “The video reveals a discrepancy between reality and Russian claims of an alleged massive advance, the encirclement of Ukrainian units and the capture of more than 65 settlements,” the author wrote.

    He noted that both vehicles operated in territory that most Russian maps mark in red — as a “Russian” zone.

    This is the same area about which we have written repeatedly. For comparison, below is a map by the Russian state agency Ria Novosti. The village of Anishchyne does not appear on it, but the settlement of Vilkhuvatka — Olkhovatka in Russian — serves as a reference point in the centre-right.

    The tank and Bradley were fighting around five km north of a location that Russia marks as securely captured.

    Drones also struck Yandex’s third data centre. Graphs circulated online, particularly on Sunday, suggesting that Ukrainian attacks on Russia’s largest internet provider had restricted the operations of Russian bots around the world.

    However, this has not yet been objectively proven. Russia has indeed reported outages affecting various internet-based services after each attack, but that is so far the only confirmed effect.

    On this occasion, French analyst Clément Molin pointed out that the Russian Varyag drone brigade had attacked data centres in Ukraine in recent weeks and had boasted, among other things, of damaging Kyivstar, Ukraine’s largest operator.

    The situation has now been reversed, as it was previously with attacks on ships and warehouses. This time, however, to Russia’s disadvantage.

    The first centre hit was in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, followed by a second in Kaluga, in the Kaluga region. On Sunday, the third of Yandex’s four largest centres was struck, this time in Vladimir, in the Vladimir region.

    “This complex houses one of the company’s Galushkin supercomputers, which is among the most powerful in Russia,” Kommersant wrote, adding that the facility had been taken out of service, affecting 10 core Yandex services, including its email service.

    The situation is serious enough that, according to digital development minister Maksut Shadayev, “Yandex is facing an unprecedented attack on its data centres”.

    The defence ministry is also working on the issue in an effort to protect the company’s remaining facilities. Citing its sources, Kommersant said replacing the damaged capacity could take up to six months.

    The battle for Dobropillia on a new type of map. As the war evolves, so do the ways it is mapped. This Ukrainian OSINT profile, for example, has depicted the fighting for the important Donbas town — which protects the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk agglomeration from the south-west — on a dynamic map.

    Among other things, it shows that Russian forces are infiltrating the town through the village of Hanivka from the Nove Shakhove area.

    For a clearer picture, we are also including a static DeepStateUA map, as the previous one is rotated and does not follow the usual compass orientation.

    The two maps are rotated by around 90 degrees in relation to each other. On the following one, Dobropillia is in the centre-left. Nove Shakhove, from where Russian infiltrators are advancing, is almost at the centre, exactly 10 km to the east as the crow flies. A small arrow directly next to the settlement’s name indicates the direction of Russian attacks.

    The green area in the upper part of the map is the so-called Dobropillia salient, which was fought over a year ago.

    Russia reported nothing significant concerning Dobropillia after the weekend. “On the Dobropillia axis, our forces continue to push forward, but Ukrainian units retain the ability to counterattack. Heavy fighting is under way,” the Two Majors wrote, for example.

    The Ukrainian Telegram channel Petrenko published a map over the weekend showing sites of new infiltrations. Its interpretation differs considerably from DeepStateUA’s version. Russian forces are shown closer to the town, but the direction of their advance is the same as in the two previous sources.

    The sites of the recorded incursions were established on the basis of videos showing drones killing Russian soldiers attempting to advance further west.

    Storm Shadow missiles caused the largest single massacre of senior Russian officers in August. On Friday (9 October), a joint project by Russian exile newspaper Meduza and the BBC’s Russian service added another 17,124 names to its list of Russian war casualties. This was the number it had counted since 21 September. In total, 276,113 Russian soldiers killed in the war are now known by name.

    On the same day, the project’s authors published a detailed analysis of events in Donetsk on 26 August. The Ukrainian air force had attacked a building in Donetsk with Storm Shadow/SCALP-EG missiles.

    The strike was so intense that the target must have been something significant. Almost immediately, there was speculation that the building housed an important Russian headquarters.

    Meduza and the BBC counted 20 high-ranking Russian military personnel killed during a joint meeting of the headquarters of the Centre group of forces and its subordinate 41st Army — 18 at the scene and another two from their injuries in the following days.

    They included seven colonels, six lieutenant colonels, five majors, one captain and one senior non-commissioned officer. They were identified thanks to access to nominal lists of headquarters staff as of 25 July and after that date.

    It also emerged that this was not the first time officers of the 41st Army had had a bad day. During an attack on 8 September 2025, it lost a lieutenant colonel, two majors and a lieutenant. The toll on 4 August 2026 was even worse, when the army lost two lieutenant colonels, three majors, two captains and one lieutenant at once.

    As Russian jet-powered drones become more widespread, videos are also appearing more frequently of Ukrainian soldiers shooting them down with man-portable air-defence systems, known by the English acronym MANPADS. This is one of them.

    Despite its best efforts, air defences at one of Russia’s ports were unable to shoot down a Ukrainian drone, which subsequently struck a Black Sea Fleet vessel. Note the beams of light used to assist with targeting.

    The Russian soldiers in this nighttime video appear relaxed. They were probably moving through an area they still considered relatively safe. But a waiting drone equipped with a thermal camera was tracking them.

    A Kyiv resident narrowly avoided a Russian drone at the last moment as it crashed into a playground.

    No update on Friday.

Of these, 19,133 (19,105) were destroyed by Ukraine, 1,003 (1,000) were damaged, 1,194 (1,194) were abandoned by their crews, and 2,840 (2,839) were captured by the Ukrainian army. This includes 4,452 (4,448) tanks, of which 3,357 (3,353) were destroyed in combat.
    • Ukraine lost 12,238 (12,175) pieces of equipment, of which 9,633 (9,579) were destroyed, 711 (702) damaged, 695 (695) abandoned and 1,199 (1,199) captured. This includes 1,466 (1,464) tanks, of which 1,126 (1,125) were destroyed in combat.

    Note: Neither side regularly reports its own dead or destroyed equipment. Ukraine publishes daily figures for Russian casualties and destroyed equipment, which cannot be independently verified. This overview uses data from the Oryx project, which has compiled a list based exclusively on photographically documented equipment losses since the start of the war.

    ]]>         ‘Made in Europe’ wind, solar, and nuclear power can protect us from future energy shocks https://euobserver.com/242252/made-in-europe-wind-solar-and-nuclear-power-can-protect-us-from-future-energy-shocks/ Mon, 12 Oct 2026 10:35:13 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=242252 Brussels is betting on a rapid build-out of homegrown renewables and nuclear to shield households and industry from the next energy shock.]]> The American humorist Will Rogers observed that there are three kinds of people in this world: those who learn by reading; those who learn by observation; and the rest, who have to learn by peeing on the electric fence for themselves.

    In Europe, we have been learning things the hard way.

    The Russian invasion of Ukraine and the resulting turmoil came as a shock to our energy system. More recently, the conflict in the Gulf has sparked fresh shock waves. 

    Having built on our experience of the energy crisis in 2022, Europe was better prepared. But the fact of the matter is that we were still left exposed to external shocks.

    Since the start of the conflict, the EU spent more than €100bn more on imported oil and gas, compared to the same period last year. We are not only learning the hard way – we are learning the expensive way.

    And the lesson could not be clearer: we need to free ourselves from fossil fuel imports, as much as possible and as soon as possible.

    The more clean energy that we produce – from homegrown sources like renewables, nuclear, and geothermal – the lower our bills become. At the same time, we also strengthen our energy security, cut our emissions, and reinforce our energy independence.

    That’s the direction we are taking

    Last year, we added 89 gigawatts of renewable energy to our energy system. One gigawatt is enough to provide electricity for up to 1m households.

    And for the first time ever, the EU produced more electricity from solar and wind than from fossil fuels.

    In other words, more of our energy is being “made in Europe”, which makes us less reliant on fossil imports. Since 2022, we have decreased our gas consumption significantly, to the order of 17 percent.

    Read more

    [Explainer] Gas glut or supply crunch? And what it means for EU methane rules

    But it’s not just about how Europe generates electricity – it’s about how we share it. Over the past decades, EU countries have linked up their electricity markets to a degree not seen elsewhere in the world.

    This makes it much easier to support each other with supplies in times of need, as well as to buy and sell electricity across borders at the best price.

    This progress has firmed up the foundations of our energy system. But can these foundations withstand our uncertain times? I believe that they can and they will – as long we stick to a solid strategy.

    Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

    EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

    Find the full transcript below: 

    European gas storage levels are unusually low for this time of year, reaching their lowest autumn level since 2011.

    With Russian gas imports set to end in 2027, could Europe face a tougher challenge in the months ahead? 

    First, how do Europe’s gas reserves work? EU countries fill underground gas storage sites during spring and summer, when demand is lower, and draw on these stocks during the winter, when heating pushes consumption up.

    Since 2022, the EU has required member states to ensure their gas storage facilities reach 90 percent of capacity by a deadline between 1 October and 1 December. That helps secure supplies ahead of winter.

    Read more

    This WEEK: Leaders to focus on economy at EU summit, in shadow of Russia threat and Middle East turmoil

    But this year, stocks are well below that target, at just over 70 percent in early October. They still have time to rise before the deadline, but the situation is attracting attention.

    Does that mean Europeans are at risk of running out of gas this winter? According to the European Commission, no. It acknowledges that storage levels are low compared with previous years, but says the EU’s gas system should still be flexible enough to meet demand this winter.

    That said, a colder or longer winter than expected, or disruptions to supplies in other parts of the world, could put additional pressure on the market. Especially at a time when the EU is preparing to phase out Russian gas imports in 2027.

    Read more

    [Explainer] Gas glut or supply crunch? And what it means for EU methane rules

    The EU has adopted a gradual ban, with transitional arrangements for existing long-term contracts.

    Russian liquefied natural gas, or LNG, is due to be phased out completely from January 2027 only. Russian gas delivered by pipeline will follow later, with the deadline set for the end of September 2027.

    And Russian gas still accounted for around 12 percent of EU gas demand through May 2026. Imports even increased in the first months of this year compared with the same period in 2025, amid disruptions to energy flows linked to the war in the Middle East.

    So, from January, Europe will lose one source of supply.  Which means Europe should try and reduce its gas consumption.

    But it’s easier said than done, particularly as winter approaches. Heating needs depend heavily on temperatures, and households cannot simply stop heating their homes.

    Read more

    G7 releases diesel stocks after Trump pressure, EU denies caving

    Still, Europe has shown in the past that consumption can fall significantly. After Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the European Commission called on member states to reduce their gas demand by 15 percent. 

    And they succeeded: their gas demand fell of around 18 percent, compared with the previous five-year average. A few months ago, following the escalation of the war in the Middle East, the Jacques Delors Institute recommended reviving efforts to reduce gas demand.

    That being said, the reduction achieved in 2022 was partly helped by a mild winter and greater use of alternative energy sources, including coal and nuclear power.

    Those options may help again, but they come with limitations. Much will depend on the weather and how long the winter lasts.

    Which doesn’t mean Europe should not call for lowering the demand and accelerate the deployment of renewable energy.

    ]]>         [Interview] Ex-Bosnia envoy sees no risk of renewed violence, but the fractured country’s EU dream is rotting away https://euobserver.com/241913/interview-ex-bosnia-envoy-sees-no-risk-of-renewed-violence-but-the-fractured-countrys-eu-dream-is-rotting-away/ Mon, 12 Oct 2026 08:32:01 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=241913 As one of Dayton’s former guardians, Schmidt fears less instability than a quiet collapse of trust, as youth reject segregated schools, politicians glorify war criminals, and Europe fails to turn Bosnia’s pro-EU mood into real opportunities.]]> Nearly three decades after the Dayton Peace Agreement ended the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the country remains deeply divided along ethnic and political lines.

    The agreement brought peace, but its complex political system has done little to overcome those divisions. Republika Srpska, the predominantly Serb entity, has pursued an increasingly divergent political course, while Serbia and Croatia maintain close ties with different parts of the country.

    And for Christian Schmidt, the international community’s high representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina (2021-26) the main threat is no longer a return to war, but political stagnation and growing frustration.

    He says that weak civic engagement, slow progress towards EU membership and the influence of Russia and neighbouring countries are reinforcing Bosnia’s divisions. Young people, he says, are increasingly responding by leaving the country.

    In this interview, Schmidt discusses foreign influence, the EU’s role, the legacy of Dayton, and why Bosnia’s future may depend on whether it can build a stronger political community across its ethnic divisions.

    A country that remains divided

    You started your work in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2021 and were there for five years. It was a period of major changes, with COVID and then the war in Ukraine. What were your experiences of these moments. How has the situation in Bosnia evolved?

    I think there has not been sufficient involvement. Civil society in Bosnia and Herzegovina is not very strong. It is, more than just politically, somehow divided on political issues. This prevents a joint political position or commitment from civil society to make more progress in democratic development and European integration.

    So far, I don’t see that this has changed very much. It has also not changed that some parties, especially the SNSD, [Serb nationalist Milorad] Dodik’s party, but honestly not only them, are counting on ethnic differences as an argument for supporting their party instead of having a multi-ethnic approach. One can be doubtful about their real pro-European commitment.

    Russia and its influence

    When civil society is not engaged and when countries are not politically stable, we know that they are prone to interference from other states or political entities. Is this being seen in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

    It is evident that neighbouring countries, especially Serbia and Croatia, have a kind of preferred relationship with parts of the country. This is, by the way, also established in the General Framework Agreement for Peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina [also known as the Dayton Peace Agreement]. So it is not necessarily something that is not in line with Dayton [Agreement].

    But there is beyond this more interference if I refer, for example, to Serbia’s reaction on the occasion of the United Nations General Assembly Resolution of 2024 about establishing an international day of commemoration for the Srebrenica genocide. There was a really remarkable attack against this, despite the fact that Serbia was not named in the resolution. There were only named individuals who had committed war crimes or genocide.

    But it was used to create a “Pan-Serbian declaration”, which can be seen as a way of bringing cultural issues of the same ethnic group closer together. It has to be seen additionally as a tool to try to gain more political influence in the other part of the country.

    You mentioned Croatia and Serbia. Is Russia also playing a role in these interferences?

    Yes, but not ethnic interference. It is more through traditional good relations, especially with the Orthodox community, which is basically the Serb Orthodox community, where there are relations and a lot of activities, including in the media and on social media.

    They [Russia] try to influence a part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, especially Banja Luka and Republika Srpska, and Dodik is somehow to act as an influencer for Russian interests. This is indeed the case. Dodik has been sitting together with [Russian president Vladimir] Putin for the 11th time since the beginning of the war in Ukraine. This is really remarkable.

    How important is Bosnia and Herzegovina and Dodik for Russia and for Putin?

    The economic and political-strategic importance is nearly zero. But it can be used as a way of distracting from European and somehow American activities, just by giving them a negative impact on everything. So this is more seen as a tool, rather than an area of influence.

    EU— only accession talks?

    Does the EU have a role in fighting such interference — Russian, but also the ethnic interference from Croatia and Serbia?

    The ethnic relationships are within the framework of Dayton, and they are acceptable. But I think it is very important that the EU makes it clear that European integration is not based on ethnic differences, but on uniting in diversity.

    This is something that is very complicated. You cannot do this only with programmes or money. I think these challenges are the typical issues that you can address through European commitment, but in the details, it has not delivered.

    Unfortunately, maybe the European Union should sit down again and think about more tools and opportunities, especially addressing civil society, to give more attraction to the European idea.

    How would that work?

      <title>Threat of AI share crash puts world financial stability at risk, says IMF</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-risk-global-imf-debt-corrowing-cyber-attacks</link>
      <description><p>High valuations and debt put sector in danger, while fund also warns on government borrowing and cyber-attacks</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/13/imf-global-economy-world-economic-outlook-uk-gdp-forecast-2026">IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’</a></p></li></ul><p>The threat of an AI share price crash rippling out across global markets is putting world financial stability at risk, the International Monetary fund has warned.</p><p>In its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Report, the IMF highlighted the sky-high valuations for AI companies along with their increasing debt pile as one reason that risks in the system are “elevated”.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/13/ai-share-crash-risk-global-imf-debt-corrowing-cyber-attacks">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>BBC asks US federal judge to compel Trump’s lawyers to schedule deposition after his team canceled initial session</p><p>The BBC is asking a federal judge in <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/florida">Florida</a> to force <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a> to sit for a deposition as part of the president’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster.</p><p>According to a Tuesday filing, the BBC and Trump’s legal team had agreed for him to be deposed on Friday.       <description><p>Martin Shkreli’s 2022 release conditions bar him from participating in the pharmaceutical industry, including ownership stakes or business decisions</p><p>The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and seven US states have alleged that pharmaceutical executive Martin Shkreli repeatedly violated a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2022/jan/14/martin-shkreli-barred-drug-industry-fined-us-court">lifetime ban</a> on participating in the pharmaceutical industry, and they are asking a judge to hold him in contempt.</p><p>In a <a href="https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2026/10/ftc-states-ask-federal-court-hold-martin-shkreli-contempt-allegedly-violating-lifetime">motion </a>filed on Tuesday in US district court in New York City, the FTC and its state co-plaintiffs allege that 43-year-old Shkreli – nicknamed the “Pharma Bro” – has traded stocks in at least 60 pharmaceutical companies and publicly commented on their businesses since his release from prison in May 2022.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/martin-shkreli-ftc-ruling-pharma-ban">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Analysts say fuel will take weeks to ship and quantity is too small to affect prices, while full deal is unlikely to be met given damage to Russian refineries</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/11/zelenskyy-trump-ukraine-russia-energy-ceasefire">Trump announces partial ceasefire but Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’</a></p></li></ul><p>Donald Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin to temporarily lift sanctions on US imports of Russian diesel will have little “meaningful” effect on motorists and businesses in the US and overseas, energy and foreign policy analysts have predicted.</p><p>The US president <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/09/trump-putin-russian-diesel-ukraine">infuriated Volodymyr Zelenskyy</a> when he announced the deal on Friday, writing on Truth Social that the agreement with his Russia counterpart to supply millions of tonnes of diesel was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared after his decision to go to war against Iran.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/11/trump-russia-diesel-deal-putin-little-impact-prices">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>US’s Reagan-era economic promises return as Trump’s AI-fueled growth fantasy</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/11/trump-ai-economy-reagan</link>
      <description><p>‘Even if AI supercharged the economy, its impact on the government’s finances would be muted’</p><p>Back through political history to the age of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ronald-reagan">Ronald Reagan</a>, Republicans have repeatedly promised the US public that tax cuts would pay for themselves, firing up economic growth and filling the government’s coffers.</p><p>The promise never really panned out. From the Gipper’s day on, the Republicans’ tax cuts inevitably increased the budget deficit. Despite its failure, though, the promise is back, coated in a fine new layer of <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/artificialintelligenceai">artificial intelligence</a> pixie dust. It will fail again.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/11/trump-ai-economy-reagan">Continue reading...</a></description>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/business/useconomy">US economy</category>

      <title>Is punishing the poor Trump’s last hand to play?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms</link>
      <description><p>The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/08/economy-midterm-elections-tell-us">Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections</a></p></li></ul><p>There is a manic quality to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a> to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.</p><p>The US president <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/28/trump-cattle-ranchers-beef-imports-backlash">offered</a> to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/23/trump-beef-imports-midterms-gop-panic-01090261">backtracking</a> under <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/25/trump-republican-backlash-beef-tariff-import">pressure</a> from the cow lobby. He <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/22/trump-diesel-export-ban">offered</a> to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/market-chatter-us-oil-executives-112235250.html">were</a> <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/chevron-ceo-diesel-export-ban-trump-supply.html">not interested</a>. He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas). In early October he started mailing <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/01/economy/trump-obamacare-500-check">$500 checks</a> to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-5000-midterm-cash-dividend-response">$5,000 check</a> if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-dividend-republican-midterm-convention">go nowhere</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Brussels uses WTO rules to quickly impose quota, which will halve Chinese market share to 3%</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/oct/12/uk-growth-inflation-pressures-oil-price-sveriges-riksbank-nobel-prize-economic-sciences-awarded-latest-news-updates">Business live – latest updates</a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/11/volkswagen-boss-backs-eu-plan-to-boost-domestic-european-industry">VW boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic industry</a></p></li></ul><p>The EU is to limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, the European Commission has confirmed.</p><p>Imports have been soaring in the past two years; about 800,000 battery and plug-in hybrids are likely to be sold this year.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/12/eu-deal-china-limit-imports-hybrid-electric-vehicles">Continue reading...</a></description>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comWed, 14 Oct 2026 11:12:12 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Work on North-South power line to start next year - Minister]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/14/work-on-north-south-power-line-to-start-next-year-minister/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/14/work-on-north-south-power-line-to-start-next-year-minister/Wed, 14 Oct 2026 10:12:56 +0000Work on a long-delayed cross-Border power line that could cut €150 million a year from electricity bills will begin next year, Minister for Climate, Environment and Energy, Darragh O’Brien pledged on Wednesday.

Planning and political controversies have delayed construction of the North-South Interconnector, a high voltage electricity line running from Co Meath to Co Tyrone that was first proposed 20 years ago.

O’Brien said on Wednesday that work should begin on the project next year as it now has full planning permission.

“It’s going to be built,” the minister stressed. He told a conference that the power line would be subject to “no more reviews”, pointing that four studies had weighed whether it was possible to run the line underground rather than on pylons.

“It will deliver reductions in energy bills of up to €150 million per annum,” O’Brien added.

He was speaking at the publication of a report by think tank, Trifecta Ireland, showing that regulations, the network and policy account for more of Irish consumers’ energy bills than the actual cost of electricity.

The Republic has the most expensive electricity in the EU, with households paying 40 cent a kilowatt hour for their power, 40 per cent more than the European average.

Trifecta Ireland has identified 17 measures that could help reduce those costs and cut electricity bills by 2030, according to the organisation’s chief executive, Conall Bolger.

For the 65 per cent of Irish adults who say they have at least one, the launch last week of a new second-hand online marketplace here by the Swedish giant will be good news.

Irish fans of the world’s biggest furniture retailer are legion. Its Ballymun shop was its best performing store globally in 2023, with some 3.2 million customers walking through the door. Total retail sales here reached €247.3 million last year, with Irish customers buying more of Ikea’s moving boxes and red wine glasses than any other country in the world.

Now, you will be able to flog your old Ikea furniture and buy preloved items on the cheap through the retailer too. So how will it work, can you make money, why is Ikea doing it – and during this Climate Action Week, is it really any good for the environment?

New marketplace

The launch of Ikea’s second-hand marketplace means customers who have signed up to the company’s Ikea Family membership scheme can connect to buy and sell pre-owned Ikea items locally. Think eBay, Vinted or Facebook Marketplace – but only for Ikea goods.

The new digital second-hand shop will make it easier for people to make some money from old Ikea furniture they no longer need, while helping others to find discounted, pre-owned items, including those no longer available in stores, says Ikea.

The only things you can’t resell are kitchen accessories, mattresses and food.

The launch here follows successful trials by the Swedish company of online second-hand marketplaces in Spain, Norway, Portugal, Poland, Sweden and Belgium.

In those countries, demand has been strongest for bedroom furniture, storage solutions and livingroom sofas and chairs. The company’s Kallax storage cubes and its Malm chest of drawers have emerged as two of the most popular items being traded second-hand to date.

Items are being listed for less than half of their full retail price, says Ikea.

“When we look at the average reduction in price for items listed, it’s 60 per cent or less,” says Greg Lucas, sustainability manager, Ikea UK and Ireland.

Got your eye on the popular Malm Storklinta chest of six drawers? These had been retailing new this summer for €160; now you could nab a set second-hand and in good nick for just €96.

That Besta TV unit that was retailing for €255? If the retailer’s predictions are correct, you could now secure a preloved model from another Ikea Family member for about €100.

Ikea has already cut its prices on about 1,500 products by between 15 and 25 per cent in 20 European countries, including Ireland, since September 1st. The move was an attempt by the flat-pack furniture retailer to counter the cost-of-living crisis as consumer confidence continues to remain depressed.

So, if you are selling products second-hand that you bought before the price drop, you may not recoup quite so much of your original spend.

Selling and buying

Unlike some second-hand marketplaces, sellers on Ikea’s site can sell for free, at least for now. Selling through some competing third-party sites can attract fees.

For example, a second-hand Ikea Kallax for sale in Ireland on Vinted right now is priced at €25, but a fee of €1.95 is charged to “cover the cost of providing a safe smooth experience for our community”, says Vinted.

Posting a product for sale on the Ikea site is arguably easier too. Sellers simply tick the product they are selling from Ikea’s vast library, and their ad will pre-populate with the exact description and dimensions, with links to spare parts. Some small spare parts are free. Sellers can also post photos of the item they have taken themselves.

“It’s down to the buyer to highlight what condition it’s in today,” says Lucas.

Helpfully, buyers can post reviews of sellers too, which should help to keep community members honest.

You can choose to receive payment by bank transfer or opt for an Ikea digital refund card – which will give sellers a 15 per cent bonus.

Sellers accepting payment via the refund card can use the credit against new Ikea products. You can also use it to buy other second-hand products in store through the company’s Buyback and Resell service.

The pleasures of Vinted have often little to do with money, although the cash is nice

This service enables customers to sell eligible products back to Ikea in exchange for in-store credit. By enabling this, Ikea may be countering criticism that the 15 per cent bonus incentivises us back into the shop to buy yet more new stuff on a planet on which there is already too much stuff.

You can also use the card to buy food at Ikea.

When an item is purchased, payment is held securely by Ikea’s payment service provider until the buyer has collected or received the item and confirms acceptance through the marketplace. At that point, a 48-hour buyer protection period begins.

During this period, the buyer can raise an issue if the product does not match its listing. For example, buyers can contact support if there are missing parts, undisclosed damage, or if the item is not an authentic Ikea product.

If there are no issues, payment is automatically released to the seller.

If there is an issue, the payment remains on hold while a refund request is reviewed in line with the marketplace’s buyer protection policy. Ikea says it can support dispute resolution where needed.

While there are no fees on the Irish site for now, the company has introduced a “buyer protection fee” in Spain, which it says supports “safeguards”, like ensuring only authentic Ikea products in usable condition are advertised and only by Ikea Family members.

Delivery

Sellers and buyers will have to arrange delivery and/or pickup between themselves. But with Ikea products so ubiquitous in Irish homes, you probably won’t have a hard time finding a Billy bookcase or Kallax cube near you.

Despite the lack of a delivery service, buying second-hand could prove more convenient than buying new. Finding a good-as-new Poang chair for sale in your own town will spare you the schlep to Ballymun, where a tour of the gargantuan shop has been known to test the most solid of relationships.

Ikea says it is “exploring” a “convenient, affordable and sustainable” delivery service for bulky items, says Lucas.

“Once the Ikea online marketplace purchase is completed, the buyer can post a ‘delivery task’, set the price they are prepared to pay for delivery and receive offers from available ‘helpers’,” says Ikea.

Ikea’s timing in Ireland is something to behold. Maybe it’s not so much the Scandi-inspired aesthetic that resonates with us so much as its ability to meet the moment. And we’ve had our moments.

Ikea opened its big blue Lego-like superstore in Dublin 11 in 2009 at the height of Ireland’s financial crash. Now, almost 20 years on from the crash, we find ourselves punch-drunk from another cost-of-living crisis and an ongoing housing crisis, and with further economic clouds scrambling on the horizon. The launch of Ikea’s second-hand selling website here on the day Budget 2027 was unveiled is well timed, or portentous.

Being able to furnish your entire home and garden affordably and from one retailer, using new or second-hand products, is not to be sniffed at. Even if everyone in your estate has the same Billy bookcase.

Slice of the pie

Second-hand shopping has become big business, and Ikea knows it. It has emerged as a “quiet but significant shift” in Irish consumer behaviour, according to analysis by RedC.

It’s no longer a niche trend confined to charity shops, vintage enthusiasts or bargain hunters. Increasingly, it is becoming a normal part of everyday consumer behaviour in Ireland, says RedC.

It’s not just a way to save money but part of a broader move towards more sustainable and circular patterns of consumption. Second-hand shopping is becoming an established part of life here.

Brands are having to rethink how they compete in a world where new products increasingly sit alongside refurbished, reused and preloved alternatives.

More than nine in 10 adults in Ireland say they shop for second-hand goods, according to research commissioned by Ikea in September. Some 45 per cent of adults said they buy pre-owned furniture.

Are you a fool to pay full price? From paint to phones, buying second-hand can slash your costs
