By incentivising payment through an Ikea digital refund card, money from transacting its products second-hand gets directed back to Ikea.

But is it green?

Buying second hand is great, says the Rediscovery Centre, the National Centre for the Circular Economy, but buying less overall, and repairing what you have, is better.

“The bigger challenge is that, in Ireland, we simply consume too much,” says Claire Downey, chief executive of the Rediscovery Centre, which is headquartered just over a kilometre from Ikea’s Ballymun outlet.

Irish homes contain an average of €531 worth of unused home and garden furniture, according to Ikea’s research, and unused home decor and accessories worth an average of €347. Yikes.

That baby changing table you bought new, and used only for a few short years, could have been borrowed.

“Many of the things we buy are not needed for long. Borrowing, sharing and renting are great alternatives to buying and they help to reduce the amount of stuff we accumulate in the first place, as well as saving money and space in our homes,” says Downey.

Ikea’s tantalising promise is that we are all just one good shoe rack away from nirvana

Circular.ie and Repairmystuff.ie are digital platforms that support communities to reduce consumption and waste by sharing, reusing and repairing, she says.

Many of the things we spend money replacing could easily be repaired, says Downey.

“We’d love to see a shift in mindset where people automatically consider repairing, renting and borrowing, or buying second-hand before buying new.”

We are still building three-bed semidetached homes in commuter towns, in a country that wants urban apartments, because the size and nature of the Irish household has changed. We are having fewer children, and more people are single and want to live alone or in a couple without necessarily wanting two extra bedrooms.

Let’s look at the first development. Prices are simply too high, and potential buyers have hit the price ceiling. The expression “the cure for high prices is high prices” is one of the oldest in economics. Eventually, very high prices fix themselves by depressing demand, because people run out of money and can’t afford to pay the higher prices. In addition, the high prices usually imply higher profits for builders and the higher prices prompt higher supply, which brings down prices in time. However, in Ireland right now, it is a simple fact that buyers are “maxed out” and can’t afford relentless rises in house prices – so they cannot play the game any longer.

Since Covid, although wages have been more or less rising in line with inflation or a small bit more, house prices across the country are up massively. In Munster, outside the cities, prices are up 72 per cent since the pandemic. They are up 62 per cent in Leinster outside Dublin; the four regional cities have seen prices rise by 57 per cent, while in Connaught/Ulster, traditionally the most moribund of housing markets, prices are up a whopping 72 per cent since Covid.

If Irish property is overvalued, will house prices fall?

Dublin lags behind, with prices up by 32 per cent in the same period. The current asking price for a three-bed semi is €635,000 in Dublin, €431,000 in Cork city, €424,000 in Galway city; €376,000 in Limerick City and €313,000 in Waterford city.

The font of all borrowing is income, so let’s look at these prices relative to wages and the ability to borrow, and then let’s see where prices should be. Real wages are roughly flat: earnings were up 3.9 per cent against inflation of 3.7 per cent last year. First-time buyers – half of all buyers – can borrow, at most, four times their income, with a 10 per cent deposit.

This is a numbers game – and the numbers don’t add up. We need far more apartments in our cities, and the asking prices for these apartments must fall

So take a couple in their 30s, both on average earnings of €1,046.88 a week, or €54,400 a year. This gives them €108,900 combined. Four times income in borrowings means a maximum mortgage of €435,500. When adding their 10 per cent deposit, the maximum purchase price they can afford is about €484,000.

Based on these figures, the Dublin family home is out of reach on their income alone. The couple would need a dual income of about €145,000 to afford the three-bed semi, or a cool €200,000 in cash.

In terms of getting an apartment in Dublin, the average two-bed costs €406,000, so it is within lending limits, and repayments are below 20 per cent of gross income. The challenge for this couple is saving up the €41,000 in cash for a deposit, roughly 4.5 months of combined gross pay.

This is not insurmountable if they have been saving, or can rely on family, and parents giving a house deposit to young couples is very common. But let’s say they would like to have a family in an urban setting, in, say, a three-bed apartment. At a cost of €502,000 it is about €18,000 over the couple’s maximum threshold, and it would require €66,500 in cash.

The Irish Times view on the ESRI housing report: house prices alarmingly overvalued

Even if taking the completely stretched first-time buying couple who’ve looked down the back of the couch to put together every cent they have, they are still well short of the needed funds in Dublin. Is it any surprise prices are adjusting in the capital?

Apologies for all the numbers in the last few paragraphs, but this is a numbers game – and the numbers don’t add up. We need far more apartments in our cities, and the asking prices for these apartments must fall. The State must fast-track building in the cities. We need to build up, because obviously the more floors in a building, the cheaper the apartments ultimately built will be – and we also need to reduce the ability of serial objectors to put spurious spanners in the works.

For now, the market has spoken – prices are adjusting downwards, because the cure for high prices is high prices.

Long may this last.

Given that these were always the terms on which the multiannual payments were based, there is as yet no clear explanation as to why the money was withheld in the first place.

None of this is good for O’Donovan’s political reputation, and there were mutterings from various unnamed Government figures over the weekend that he might not keep his Cabinet seat when the midterm reshuffle takes place at the end of next year.

The Limerick TD seems to have an unfortunate knack for losing friends and alienating people, but last week’s embarrassments and the subsequent clean-up may have forced the question of how RTÉ is funded back on to the agenda, and that would not be a bad thing.

The current arrangement was agreed by the previous government in the summer of 2024. It guaranteed RTÉ €725 million in public money over three years, rising from €225 million in 2025 to €240 million this year and €260 million in 2027. The licence fee was retained, and the Exchequer committed to making up the difference between what it brought in and the agreed total. The lower amount raised from licence revenue, the bigger the cheque from the State.

That difference is growing quickly. Licence sales have fallen every year since the 2023 payments scandal. Figures released by O’Donovan last week show sales down 6 per cent in the first nine months of this year, putting full-year income on course for about €114 million, compared with more than €150 million in 2022.

Less widely understood is how much of the licence fee the State already pays. The Department of Social Protection funds free licences for everyone over 70 and others who qualify for the household benefits package, a bill in excess of €80 million a year. That is more than 500,000 licences, set against roughly 715,000 bought by households this year.

Free licences grow by up to 20,000 a year as the population ages, while paid ones keep falling. Remarkably, if current trends hold, licences paid for by social protection will outnumber those paid for by households as early as 2029. This seems untenable.

Does Patrick O’Donovan’s explanation for €20m RTÉ funding cut add up?

Add the direct top-up and the picture is starker still. In 2025, about 54 per cent of RTÉ’s public funding came from the Exchequer in one form or another. By 2027, that share is likely to be above 60 per cent. The licence fee survives in name, but the money increasingly comes directly from Government.

European law now has something to say about this. The European Media Freedom Act requires member states to fund public broadcasters through transparent procedures based on objective criteria set in advance, and to ensure they have “adequate, sustainable and predictable” resources. The point is to protect editorial independence by making sure money cannot be used as a political lever. The Broadcasting (Amendment) Bill now before the Oireachtas is meant to give effect to those rules here.

Last week’s episode looks much more like political incompetence than a deliberate act of interference. But cutting an agreed sum at a few hours’ notice, without explanation, is clearly not in keeping with the spirit of the EU rules. Whatever its cause, it has shown how easily the money can be turned on and off.

Nor should the role of ill-will be underestimated. Members of the Oireachtas media committee have indicated they intend to question RTÉ director general Kevin Bakhurst about a newspaper column by radio presenter Oliver Callan, which questioned Simon Harris’s credentials as Minister for Finance. One source described Callan’s piece as “antigovernment”. Whether a presenter’s newspaper column should be a matter for a committee examining RTÉ’s finances is debatable. That the two are being raised alongside each other is telling.

The new legislation will strengthen the role of Coimisiún na Meán, which will assess RTÉ’s needs and recommend a level of funding for each three-year period. But the regulator’s role will be advisory. There will be no legal obligation on the minister of the day to follow its recommendations, nor, as far as can be seen, any requirement to explain a decision not to. The final call will remain where it was last week, with a politician putting together a budget.

The licence fee has many faults, including the fact that it is now collapsing before our eyes. But it was based on a sound principle. Money paid directly by citizens to a public service broadcaster, at arm’s length from the government of the day, gave that broadcaster a degree of independence that an annual grant cannot.

If public service broadcasting is to retain public trust and integrity, it must be insulated from political pressure, whether born of malice or just haplessness. If nothing else, we can thank O’Donovan for reminding us of that.

]]>Beeldbewerking<![CDATA[Is my €1,000 monthly childcare bill really falling to €550?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/13/is-my-1000-monthly-childcare-bill-really-falling-to-550/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/13/is-my-1000-monthly-childcare-bill-really-falling-to-550/Tue, 13 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000I pay €1,000 per month for creche (full time). What is the Budget 2027 impact here? I saw a headline suggesting childcare was being reduced to €550 per month up to senior infants but I can’t imagine that’s right. UM

Getting your head around childcare costs can be fiendishly complex. There are different subsidies depending on your financial status and the age of the child and different bands depending on how long the child is in care.

And if it is any consolation, it is not just you and other parents who get confused. In his speech, the Minister for Public Expenditure and Reform, Jack Chambers, did say he was “reducing the maximum childcare fees paid by parents, from €735 to €550 per month for children up to senior infants”, putting €2,200 a year back into parents’ pockets.

Not quite – at least not for everyone, including you. But that does not mean there was not good news for you on childcare in the budget – at least from September of next year when the budget childcare measures kick in.

The Minister was referring to the maximum amount a parent of a child receiving between 40 and 50 hours of care a week can be charged in a creche that has signed up to the Government’s “core funding” scheme, where Government subsidises the cost of care. This is called Band E.

If you are paying €1,000 – or more accurately €959 – a month, you will be in Band F, where your child is receiving care for more than 50 hours a week.

And you are far from alone in having been taken aback by talk of the €735 and €550 maximums.

The Minister’s team insist that Band E is the one most commonly used by parents across the State. That may be so; the statement was not accompanied by figures. What does seem certain is that most parents in Dublin and some surrounding commuter counties, as well as areas of Cork and Galway, are paying Band F fees like you.

Budget 2027’s childcare package has triggered storm of protest from parents. Here’s why

The net cost to you is determined by two things: fee per band and the personal subsidy to which each child is entitled, depending on your income.

Under the budget measures, the fee for Band F will fall from €336 a week to €300. And, for those on the universal subsidy (anyone with family income of more than €73,000), the subsidy for children up to senior infants will rise to €2.50 from €2.15 per hour up to a maximum of 45 hours.

If your income is below €73,000, the subsidy may be higher and, if it is below €36,500, that could be as high as €5.10 an hour.

When they say household income, they mean income minus any pension contributions you pay. You also do not include certain welfare payments and, if you have more than one child, there are further income disregards.

Anyway, back to the numbers. That €2.50 an hour universal subsidy amounts to €112.50 a week. Taking this from your €300 “fee”, you are left with €187.50. From September next year (11 months in the future), that will be your weekly fee, amounting to €750 a month.

That means a fall of at least €209 in your childcare cost per child each month, or somewhere between €2,300 and €2,500 over the year. So good news, if not quite a drop in charge to €550.

Of course, that is only if you are in a creche that operates under Government core funding. If not, they are free to charge what the market will bear.

]]><![CDATA[Ireland’s infrastructure shortfalls hit firms’ finances]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/13/infrastructure-shortfalls-hit-firms-finances/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/13/infrastructure-shortfalls-hit-firms-finances/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 23:01:00 +0000Ireland’s infrastructure shortfalls are damaging businesses’ finances by driving up costs or hindering efforts to hire workers, most managers believe.

Government plans to spend €250 billion tackling gaps in the State’s water, energy and transport systems, and to speed up house building.

But the challenges posed by poor infrastructure are hindering business and pose a threat to growth, a survey by the Institute of Directors (IoD), showed.

More than 70 per cent of members said that deficits in housing, energy, water, transport and broadband are damaging their organisation’s finances, according to the study.

A third of members said the problems hinder their ability to hire or keep staff. Housing and energy are the leading causes of concern, followed by transport, the survey showed.

Businessman Seán O’Driscoll, a member of the Government’s Accelerating Infrastructure Taskforce, who will address the institute’s conference on Tuesday, welcomed the Budget 2027 pledge to invest in the State’s infrastructure.

But he cautioned that the Republic still faced “deep-seated” challenges when it came to completing vital infrastructure projects on time and within their budgets.

“Our infrastructure deficit isn’t a lack of ambition or talent; it is the result of two decades of failing to plan for our own success,” he said ahead of the conference.

Confusion in business about looming State rules on AI

O’Driscoll branded as worrying business people’s fears that shortfalls are hitting the finances of their companies.

“If we want to safeguard Ireland’s long-term competitiveness and deliver the housing, energy, water and transport systems a growing economy requires, we need clear accountability, faster decision-making, and a willingness to accept and manage risk, rather than being paralysed by it,” he argued.

The IoD’s survey of 427 directors and managers found that more than three in four of them expected growth next year, with 37 per cent of them planning to hire staff and half intending to maintain current employment.

IoD chief executive Caroline Spillane argued that Government should match managers’ plans to grow by cutting the cost of doing business and lowering barriers that hold firms back.

“As we digest the impact of Budget 2027, it is very striking that well over half of business leaders do not feel the business provisions outlined in the previous budget last year have been able to boost competitiveness a full year on,” Spillane said.

About two thirds of business people do not believe that the State has become a more competitive location in which to invest since Budget 2026, the study showed.

O’Driscoll, a former chairman of industrial group Glen Dimplex and the Economic and Social Research Institute, will address the conference, titled Leading in Governance, in Dublin’s Intercontinental Hotel.

Other speakers include Kara Owen, British Ambassador to Ireland, and Prof Stephen Kinsella, economic adviser to Tánaiste Simon Harris.

Survey highlights wide gaps in pay for non-executive directors

]]>Provision<![CDATA[Investment vehicle sues over financing plan for apartment scheme in Leopardstown]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/10/12/investment-vehicle-sues-over-south-dublin-apartment-scheme-financing-plan/https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/10/12/investment-vehicle-sues-over-south-dublin-apartment-scheme-financing-plan/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 17:12:32 +0000A corporate investment vehicle set up to acquire a residential site in south Dublin is suing a company over alleged misrepresentation as to projected returns and non-disclosure of an aggregate promoter fee.

Merleview Ltd has brought Commercial Court proceedings against Burton Carman Ltd, a special purpose vehicle set up to acquire, hold and develop a property at Leopardstown Park with a view, it is claimed, to develop around 145 build-to-rent apartments. It is also suing Elkstone Capital Partners Ltd, which was the promoter and manager of the investment in Burton Carman.

The defendants deny the claims.

The case was entered to the fast track Commercial Court on Monday by Judge Eileen Roberts on consent between the parties.

It was adjourned to next month after the judge was told there may be mediation or alternatively, the defendants say, the dispute may be covered by an arbitration clause.

In a sworn statement seeking entry of the case to the commercial list, Andrew Murphy, a director of Merleview, said that in February 2022, Elkstone director and chief revenue officer Ruairí O’Neill presented him with an “equity opportunity pitch deck” and a “debt opportunity pitch deck” concerning the development of the Leopardstown property. It was proposed to develop it as a private rental sector scheme of around 145 apartments.

Murphy said the pitch decks forecast an exit value of €14.9 million, an equity return of 42 per cent IRR (internal rate of return) and a 2.01 times multiple on a €2.9 million equity investment over 24 months along with a senior debt coupon of 10 per cent a year.

On the strength of these representations, Murphy said, Merleview subscribed for ordinary shares in Burton Carman and advanced an accompanying senior debt facility, together totalling €446,969.

In July 2023, Merleview advanced a further amount of some €303,000 as a loan note.

Murphy said the executed loan note certificate stated an interest rate of 7.5 per cent per annum even though the “debt deck”, and O’Neill’s own representations, had put the rate at 10 per cent.

In August, the defendants’ solicitors sent a corrected certificate showing an interest rate of 10 per cent on the loan note from March 2023 and acknowledging the original cert had been wrong in relation to that.

In April 2026, Merleview raised 10 categories of complaint against Elkstone including misrepresentation as to projected returns and the interest rate and non-disclosure of an aggregate promoter fee entitlement of some €781,000, which Murphy said was equivalent to 15.5 per cent of the total capital raised of some €5 million.

There was also an unauthorised material change to the investment strategy from a private rental sector scheme to a build-to-sell scheme without the investor majority consent required, Murphy said.

There was also a breach of ongoing reporting obligations under the subscription and shareholders agreement (SSA), he added.

The defendants’ solicitors denied liability and that Elkstone owed Merleview no duty of care given the disclaimers in the pitch decks and the SSA.

Merleview issued proceedings last August claiming recovery of the €303,000 principal sum under the loan note, damages for breach of duty, and for intentional interference with Merleview’s economic interests.

Murphy said it was important the proceedings be resolved without delay as Merleview’s senior debt and loan notes have been in default since July 2025 and no principal has been repaid to date. Interest continues to accrue, he said.

Despite repeated requests, he said, the defendants have not produced audited accounts, management reports or verified fee accounts and the parties are in dispute as to Merleview’s entitlement under the SSA to withhold consent to certain proposed transactions pending provision of the information.

The defendants’ solicitors have also indicated an intention to apply for security for costs against Merleview. However, Merleview says it is a fully solvent company.

]]>w-ings<![CDATA[Sky Ireland revenue rises with help from Rory McIlroy 2025 Masters win]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/skys-irish-revenues-rise-helped-by-rory-mcilroys-masters-win/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/skys-irish-revenues-rise-helped-by-rory-mcilroys-masters-win/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 16:12:16 +0000Rory McIlroy’s winning putt in the 2025 Masters at Augusta last year helped the Irish arm of Sky to increase revenue by 7 per cent to £539 million (€637 million).

Accounts lodged by Sky Subscribers Services at Companies House in the UK show Sky’s Ireland business rose by £35 million from £504 million to £539 million last year.

Sky Sports recorded its highest ever Sunday viewership in April 2025 when McIlroy clinched his Masters win in dramatic circumstances.

Sky’s Irish revenue relates to revenue from direct-to-home pay television, broadband, mobile and telephony subscriptions in Ireland.

The revenue increase was also helped by Sky Ireland imposing a 4.5 per cent price hike on average for Sky customers here.

Sky Broadband has about 280,000 customers, giving it a 17 per cent market share with Sky Ireland’s market share across fibre-to-the-home broadband reaching 21.4 per cent based on the latest ComReg figures.

Sky Broadband has now delivered more than 50 consecutive quarters of customer growth.

Earlier this year, in its battle against the piracy of Sky channels through so-called dodgy boxes, the company issued about 200 cease-and-desist letters to individuals.

Details of 300 ‘dodgy box’ users to be provided to Sky, High Court hears

The vast majority of the individuals who were served letters are in Co Wexford and it is understood that the compliance level has been high on receipt of the letters.

A spokesman for Sky Ireland said today: “Sky invests significantly in protecting our content, which can include taking action against those who watch Sky without paying the proper subscription fee.

“For those individuals who received cease-and-desist letters earlier in the year, who did not return undertakings, we are moving towards further action. This may include, where necessary, seeking court injunctions to prevent continued use of illegal IPTV services and pursuing damages for copyright infringement and legal costs.”

Overall revenue at Sky Subscribers Services Ltd in 2025 increased by 5.6 per cent from £1.012 billion to £1.069 billion as pretax profit declined by 12 per cent to £97 million.

]]>Richard Heathcote<![CDATA[Aviva expands flood insurance access to 13,000 properties following ‘granular’ map update]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/aviva-expands-flood-insurance-access-to-13000-properties-following-granular-map-update/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/aviva-expands-flood-insurance-access-to-13000-properties-following-granular-map-update/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 17:44:20 +0000Aviva has increased access to flood protection insurance for an additional 13,000 homes and businesses across the State following reforms to its “extremely granular” flood risk map, the insurer said.

The enhancement comes two months after the Government established its Flood Insurance Protection Gap Working Group, of which Aviva, one of the largest general insurance providers in the Irish market, is a member.

This move “is a positive example of the progress being made through investment in flood protection measures, improved understanding of risk and greater collaboration across stakeholders,” said Joanie Hughes, managing director of personal lines at Aviva.

Julie Frazer, head of product, underwriting and intermediary within the personal lines division, said Aviva was “constantly updating its risk assessments” and “regularly reviews data” to do with flood risk.

She said recent “severe weather events”, such as Storm Chandra and Storm Eowyn, “absolutely inform our decisions” on the matter.

The insurer has since updated its “extremely granular maps ... based on the probability of a flood event occurring” at any given property, she said.

The 13,000 additional properties are “very much widespread right across the country.

“Flood risk can be really localised”, with the rock type, hill incline, and proximity to a body of water all factors that can result in “one property being able to access flood protection and another one ‘just up the road’ not,” Frazer continued.

ESB battens down the hatches for storm season

“Needless to say, the flood protection gap is something we’re very conscious of and would like to help to close,” she went on, “it’s very much at the forefront of our minds.”

Market research conducted by 3Gem Research & Insights on behalf of Aviva “reveals growing awareness among homeowners of the risks posed by extreme weather”, the insurer said.

While it found one-in-10 homeowners have experienced flood damage in the past five years, 24 per cent have experienced “storm-related damage”, and 62 per cent are “concerned” of extreme-weather damage over the next five years.

“Despite high levels of awareness and concern, almost half of homeowners (46 per cent) have not made any improvements to protect their property from extreme weather over the past two years,” Aviva said.

Common actions taken include upgrading gutter systems, repairing roofs, purchasing emergency kits and improving drainage systems, the research of 1,000 homeowners found.

Aviva advised homeowners to inform themselves of weather warnings and local flood risks through alerts from Met Éireann and to consider implementing “practical reliance measures” such as flood barriers to their properties.

The Government established in August a flood insurance working group. Tánaiste Simon Harris said “it will bring together the key public and private sector stakeholders needed to identify practical solutions to one of the most challenging issues facing the insurance market”.

“We have been very much involved with this alongside all of our peers in the industry,” Frazer said. “We’re very determined to find a way to deal with the flood protection gap – we understand and appreciate the difficulties it can create for homeowners and business owners,” she said.

]]>Leah Farrell<![CDATA[European stocks rise with banks proving a safe bet]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/european-stocks-rise-with-banks-proving-a-safe-bet/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/european-stocks-rise-with-banks-proving-a-safe-bet/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 17:07:31 +0000Stocks across Europe largely rose on Monday, bolstered by investor confidence in the banking sectors and strong returns by drinks and luxury giants.

Close to home, banking also proved a safe investment as Dublin’s stock market saw positive returns from financial groups, manufacturers and construction companies alike.

Across the Atlantic, however, many traders were hesitant to begin the week with a strong start as key inflation data looms later in the week, seen to be pivotal in shaping the Federal Reserve’s economic forecasts and the trajectory of interest rates.

DUBLIN

The Iseq All-Share index rose 1.60 per cent to start the week in the green, closing at 14,123.87 following positive results in the banking and manufacturing sectors.

Strong gains by the building materials and insulation manufacturer Kingspan, whose share price rose 2.41 per cent to €101.80 by close of business, were among the day’s top results.

Elsewhere, home builder Glenveagh Properties was up 1.77 per cent to close at €2.30 a share, while Cairn Homes grew by 0.03 per cent to close at €2.64. Food technology company Kerry Group also saw strong returns, up 1.45 per cent at €88.70 a share.

Both major banks traded on the index saw their share price increase. Bank of Ireland was up 1.79 per cent to close at €18.46, while rival AIB lagged slightly behind, up 1.68 per cent to finish at €10.86.

Agri-services group Origin Enterprises and healthcare company Uniphar also saw their share prices increase, 3.95 per cent and 3.26 per cent to €3.95 and €3.97 a share, respectively.

Insurer FBD Holdings saw its share price drop, down 1.84 per cent to €18.65 by the end of the trading day.

LONDON

The London stock market saw stocks largely rise across the board, with its blue-chip FTSE 100 index increasing 0.99 per cent and the mid-cap FTSE 250 up 0.47 per cent as well.

Investors put their trust in British banks, with Lloyds Banking Group rising 2.36 per cent and Barclays not far behind, up 1.85 per cent by close. Meanwhile, Lion Finance also jumped 2.75 per cent.

Guinness-brewer Diageo, who also owns Smirnoff Vodka and Don Julio tequila, ended the day up 2.14 per cent on Friday’s closing price.

Telecommunications group Vodafone, however, dipped 1.39 per cent by close – as did publishing and exhibitions group Informa, whose share price fell 2.41 per cent.

EUROPE

Elsewhere in Europe, investors in banking portfolios and luxury goods suppliers helped the continent’s two major indices also close the trading day with growth.

The Stoxx 600 index was up 0.65 per cent, while the Stoxx 50 followed, up 0.45.

Spain’s Santander bank increased 1.80 per cent, while German Deutsche Telekom rose 1.13 per cent.

Elsewhere, France’s luxury good giant Hermes International soared 2.10 per cent by close. Car manufacturer Mercedes Benz Group, however, saw its share price dip 0.82 per cent.

NEW YORK

Early trades on Wall Street pointed to a slightly less positive trend compared with global indices.

Some stocks fluctuated near their all-time highs while others faltered as traders looked ahead to the start of the earnings season.

Before midday New York time, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 0.43 per cent, meanwhile the S&P saw little change and the Nasdaq fell some 0.60 per cent.

Most companies in the S&P 500 rose despite renewed losses in chipmakers and looming inflation data to be released later this week that will be key in shaping the Federal Reserve’s outlook. – Additional reporting: Bloomberg.

]]>Karsten Moran<![CDATA[OpenAI to create 200 jobs in Dublin]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/openai-to-create-200-jobs-in-dublin/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/openai-to-create-200-jobs-in-dublin/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 15:35:23 +0000Artificial intelligence company OpenAI is to create 200 jobs in Ireland, with plans for a new applied AI lab at what is its European Union headquarters.

OpenAI tells investors revenue run rate is $20bn below earlier indication

]]><![CDATA[Supreme Court rejects application to appeal plan for data centre in Ennis]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/supreme-court-rejects-application-to-appeal-plan-for-data-centre-in-ennis/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/supreme-court-rejects-application-to-appeal-plan-for-data-centre-in-ennis/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 15:24:32 +0000

The Supreme Court has dismissed an application by opponents of a 200MW €1.6 billion data centre on the outskirts of Ennis for leave to appeal against a High Court decision, clearing all legal hurdles faced by the project.

In its determination, the Supreme Court has dismissed the three grounds put forward in the application by opponents of the data centre, namely Colin Doyle, Friends of the Irish Environment CLG, Futureproof Clare, Martin Knox and Christine Sharp.

The Supreme Court found the application did not meet the constitutional threshold required for leave to be granted to appeal the High Court upholding the planning permission granted by An Coimisiún Pleanála (ACP) to Art Data Centres Ltd.

In its determination, the Supreme Court found that “no point of general public importance arises” in the grounds put forward by the appellants.

ACP granted planning permission in April 2024 to Art Data Centres Ltd comprising six data halls covering 145 acres or 1.3 million sq ft on lands adjacent to the Tulla Road on the eastern outskirts of Ennis near Junction 13 on the M18 motorway connecting Galway to Limerick.

The project is set to generate up to 1,200 jobs during construction, and up to a 1,000 permanent jobs and the underpinning of thousands more in digital industries.

On Monday, the joint founders of Art Data Centres, Tom McNamara and Vincent Fogarty, said the ruling “recognises that there is a future for environmentally-sensitive data centre developments like ours, where there is responsible use of renewable energy, grid-supporting generation technology and heat-recycling for both agri-food and local heating schemes”.

They described the Supreme Court ruling as “great news for this data centre campus and for Clare as the project will be a key pillar of the Ennis 2040 Economic Plan for the area”.

The project’s 200MW scale “will be attractive to the largest technology partners in the world and the project represents the culmination of more than ten years of preparatory work”, they said.

They said the connection applications could be finally processed following the Supreme Court ruling “and work will commence in 2027 as soon as all is in place”.

]]><![CDATA[Takeover panel rejects PTSB sale complaints from ex-banker ]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/financial-services/2026/10/12/takeover-panel-rejects-ptsb-sale-complaints-from-ex-banker/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/financial-services/2026/10/12/takeover-panel-rejects-ptsb-sale-complaints-from-ex-banker/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 09:48:30 +0000The Irish Takeover Panel has rejected concerns raised about the PTSB sale process from a firm cofounded by boom-time Irish banker Mark Duffy, which has also indicated it is considering an 11th-hour bid for the bank.

Axis Capital, an advisory business cofounded by former Bank of Scotland (Ireland) chief executive Duffy, sent a letter to the panel on July 27th that consolidated “a number of matters” it had previously raised in relation to the proposed €1.62 billion acquisition of PTSB by Austrian banking group Bawag.

The panel said that “having carefully considered the substance of all of the matters raised by Axis”, it has ruled there was no case laid out that amounted to any breach of Irish takeover rules.

The announcement comes just weeks before the High Court, which is overseeing the so-called scheme-of-arrangement deal for PTSB to be sold to Bawag, is due to hold its sanctioning hearing on October 27th.

Axis made an intervention on October 2nd saying it was considering making a bid for PTSB. Last Friday, a long-term dissenting PTSB shareholder, Scotchstone Capital, led by Piotr Skoczylas, also said it was weighing a bid for PTSB. Neither has confirmed whether it has secured any funding for a bid.

Axis is being advised by Quirin Privatbank in Berlin and law firm Belmont Legal in Frankfurt.

Axis helped initiate talks in 2025 between New York private equity firm Centerbridge, the Department of Finance and PTSB over a potential deal for the Irish bank. The US group subsequently submitted a non-binding proposal in September last year for the State’s 57.5 per cent stake in the bank.

Centerbridge was the underbidder to Bawag in April as a formal sales process, initiated in October, concluded.

Axis was reported by the Business Post in July to have been urging minority shareholders to vote against the planned Bawag deal at an extraordinary general meeting (egm) later that month. Axis said in a note circulated to shareholders it had become “increasingly uncomfortable with the way the process has developed”, claiming there had been “inordinate involvement from one shareholder, leaving others effectively as bystanders”.

In July, Duffy said in a post on LinkedIn, the professional social networking platform, that the panel should reopen the sale process to allow “all credible bidders to make their best and final bids to all shareholders”.

PTSB secured backing from 91.3 per cent of shareholders – led by the Government – for the Bawag takeover at the July egm. However, some 36 per cent of minority investors voted against the transaction at the meeting.

It is expected the High Court will be asked by some minority shareholders to order the holding of a separate vote of minority investors. PTSB has repeatedly said it had “very strong” legal advice that only one vote was necessary.

]]><![CDATA[DAA says staff in Saudi Arabia ‘safe and well’ after latest airport attacks]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/daa-says-staff-in-saudi-arabia-safe-and-well-after-latest-airport-attacks/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/12/daa-says-staff-in-saudi-arabia-safe-and-well-after-latest-airport-attacks/Mon, 12 Oct 2026 13:28:32 +0000Dublin Airport operator DAA has said that all of its staff in Saudi Arabia are “safe and well” after Yemen’s Houthi forces launched more attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh in recent days.

The Irish commercial semi-state company provides airport management and consultancy services to the operator of the Saudi international travel hub.

An attack on the airport on Saturday, the third in a week, killed 12 people and wounded more than 300, part of a tit-for-tat military escalation by the Houthis against the Saudis.

Separately, an unidentified projectile hit a passenger terminal at the airport on Sunday, with authorities tackling a blaze, the Saudi-led coalition said in a statement.

In a statement on Monday, a spokesman for DAA said: “We are aware of the incidents at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh over the weekend and can confirm that all our team members in the region are safe and well. We remain in close and continuous contact with our colleagues and are monitoring the situation closely.”

DAA declined to say how many staff it has in Saudi Arabia due to commercial sensitivities and security considerations.

The blast at the Riyadh airport on Saturday brought travel to a near-standstill. It also forced the capital’s financial hub to shift to remote work until further notice and prompted executives from BP and Shell to pull out of a big energy event in the city this week.

The Department of Foreign Affairs “strongly advises Irish citizens against all but essential travel to Saudi Arabia until further notice” due to the security situation in the Middle East and Gulf.

‘They’re not just guys in flip-flops’: Houthis show military reach with deadly missile strikes on Riyadh

Irish citizens already in the region are advised to avoid “unnecessary journeys, remain vigilant, closely monitor developments and local media, and follow the advice of local authorities”.

The UK government warned on Sunday against all but essential travel to Jeddah and Dammam, as well as to all Saudi airports except for Medina. It suggested British citizens consider departing Saudi Arabia via land to neighbouring countries.

Saturday’s strike came less than a week after Saudi-backed forces in Yemen launched a campaign to retake Houthi-held areas and “eliminate” the group. The militants, who frequently claim attacks on Saudi oil facilities, had recently seized more Yemeni territory and bolstered their control over the Bab el-Mandeb, a global shipping chokepoint.

The Saudi-led coalition called “the cowardly terrorist attack” on the airport on Saturday “a full-fledged war crime” by the Houthis.

The victims included four Saudis, a Palestinian, two Bangladeshis and one person each from the US, Egypt, Jordan, Syria and Sudan, according to authorities. – Additional reporting: Bloomberg

Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg has announced plans to build a new factory in Poland producing counter-drone systems. The firm will invest over 200 million zloty (€46 million) in the facility, creating more than 100 long-term jobs.

“The new facility will support Polish industry and defence capabilities and strengthen Kongsberg’s presence in Poland,” declared CEO Eirik Lie alongside Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz at the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year serving as the official partner nation.

In January, Kongsberg signed an agreement to supply a new anti-drone system to Poland in partnership with Polish state defence group PGZ. The project comes in response to growing fears over the threat of Russian drones, around 20 of which violated Polish airspace on one night in September last year.

Norwegowie inwestują w Polsce. Duża inwestycja #Kongsberg na Pomorzu ogłoszona właśnie na #WSF2026. Szybka budowa fabryki i nowe miejsca pracy. pic.twitter.com/msI2FWGym8

— Beata Górka-Winter (@BeataGWinter) October 12, 2026

Kosiniak-Kamysz thanked Kongsberg for its investment and emphasised that Polish-Norwegian relations are at their highest point in history, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

The announcement of the counter-drone plant came as Poland and Norway’s prime ministers, Donald Tusk and Jonas Gahr Støre, signed a declaration on strategic partnership that pledged to deepen security ties, including joint defence production and strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks.

While the exact location of the plant has not been revealed, Kongsberg stated that it would be in northern Poland, near the Tricity area (consisting of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot) on the Baltic Sea coast.

Construction of the facility is scheduled to begin this year, with production at the site scheduled to commence in the first half of 2028.

 

Counter-drone technology has become an increasing priority for Poland following Russian airspace violations and also the growing use by Moscow of jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border, including recently a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw.

Polish spending on drones and counter-drone systems combined rose from 100 million zloty in 2023 to 26 billion zloty in 2026, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk announced in August, quoted by news website Interia.

The summary report of this week’s Warsaw Security Forum suggested the use of counter-drone systems to create a “controlled fly-zone” over the Suwałki Gap, a strategically important choke point along the Polish-Lithuanian border that sits between the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and Russia’s ally Belarus.

Poland has signed an agreement for a new anti-drone system that it claims will be the first of its kind in Europe.

The network is intended to protect Poland’s eastern borders, where last year around 20 Russian drones crossed in an unprecedented incursion https://t.co/WhWhJxDwXA

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 30, 2026

Poland has in recent years moved to strengthen its defence ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland.

In 2024, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab.

Saab this year also signed a strategic collaboration agreement with PGZ that will see them cooperate on naval production, servicing and technology.

On Monday this week, Norway’s defence ministry announced that Poland will join an initiative recently launched by 11 European countries and Canada to cooperate more closely on security in the North Atlantic, Arctic and Baltic Sea.

]]> New Polish constitutional court judge takes oath in defiance of president https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/14/new-polish-constitutional-court-judge-takes-oath-in-defiance-of-president/ Wed, 14 Oct 2026 08:52:44 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105505

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.

The standoff between the government and opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki over Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom Prime Minister Donald Tusk recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president.

Berek is now the fifth judge to take their oath without presidential approval. The previous four have been denied entry to the TK, and speculation is rife that the government may soon take action to ensure that the excluded judges are able to take up their positions.

PILNE 🚨 dr Maciej Berek złożył w Sejmie ślubowanie na sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego! pic.twitter.com/sZlzLnsL3M

— Bogdan Zdrojewski (@BZdrojewski) October 14, 2026

Under Polish law, a new TK judge must swear an oath “before the president”. However, since Berek was elected to the TK by the government’s majority in parliament in early September, Nawrocki has refused to swear him in.

The president claims that Berek has not presented evidence that he meets the statutory requirement of having practiced as a legal counsel for at least 10 years. Berek says he has done so.

Nawrocki has also expressed his opposition to the fact that Berek has gone from serving in Tusk’s cabinet, where he was minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy, to becoming a TK judge.

Even some members of Tusk’s ruling coalition opposed Berek’s candidacy, saying that it contradicted the government’s earlier pledges to “depoliticise” the judicial system, including by banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge.

 

With no invitation from Nawrocki forthcoming, on Wednesday morning Berek instead swore his oath at a ceremony organised in parliament. He declared that he was directing the oath towards the president, despite Nawrocki not being present.

The development came a day after the Venice Commission, an advisory body to the Council of Europe on constitutional law, had issued an opinion effectively supporting the government’s position on the crisis around the TK.

The commission found that the Polish president should swear in TK judges chosen by parliament “without delay” and does not have the power to review their election. It added that, if the president refuses to receive a judge’s oath, they are justified in taking it without him being present.

The opinion was welcomed by Tusk and his government. However, Nawrocki’s spokesman, Rafał Leśkiewicz, pointed out that the Venice Commission’s opinions are advisory and not legally binding.

1294/2026

Poland – Opinion on the powers of the President in the context of the oath-taking of the judges of the Constitutional Tribunal and of other judicial appointments.https://t.co/vcpfNeteWo

— Radoslaw Szewczyk (@SzewczykRadek) October 13, 2026

Earlier this year, four other TK judges chosen by parliament similarly organised their own swearing-in ceremony in parliament after Nawrocki failed to invite them to take their oaths before him.

However, when they arrived at the TK to take up their positions, they were prevented from doing so by the court’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government (and had previously served as a minister in that government).

Święczkowski argues that the judges cannot take up their positions unless they swear an oath in the presence of Nawrocki, who was elected as president last year with the support of PiS.

In May, the European Court of Human Rights ordered that the four judges be accepted onto the TK. However, Święczkowski has so far refused to comply, arguing that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision.

In a further escalation of the crisis around Poland's constitutional court, prosecutors have charged two officials for preventing new judges from taking up their positions.

Meanwhile, the chief justice has launched proceedings against three other judges https://t.co/aeKKue37oN

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 24, 2026

Since replacing PiS in office in December 2023, Tusk’s government has refused to recognise the legitimacy of the TK, pointing to the fact that some of its judges were unlawfully appointed under PiS. It has ignored all rulings issued by the tribunal.

Until this year, the ruling coalition refused to fill new vacancies that resulted from the expiration of judges’ nine-year terms or their retirement. However, that position changed in March, when it began filling the backlog.

So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its candidates in theory now have a majority on the 15-person court. However, Nawrocki has only sworn in three of those judges, with the other refused entry to the TK.

Prime Minister @donaldtusk has succeeded in having Maciej Berek, whom he recently described as his “right-hand man”, elected by parliament as a constitutional court judge, staving off a rebellion from some members of his own coalition https://t.co/VAVbkGL8xS

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 4, 2026

Speculation has been rife that the government will take action to ensure that the excluded judges can gain access to the court, perhaps even using the police to force entry.

Speaking to broadcaster Polsat today, justice minister Waldemar Żurek said that “the state must do everything to enable these judges to adjudicate”. He added that Berek’s swearing-in “brings us much closer to launching the tribunal’s work”.

However, Nawrocki’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, told Polsat that today’s ceremony in parliament was “grotesque” and “a sad day for Polish democracy”.

This morning has also seen some clashes between police and supporters of PiS and Nawrocki, who have been camped out outside the TK in order to defend it from any takeover by force.

❗️Policja szarpie posłów oraz zgromadzonych obywateli pod TK ❗️ pic.twitter.com/eGPRFQJnAX

— Oskar Szafarowicz (@Szafarowicz2001) October 14, 2026

]]> Man charged with plotting attack on Polish PM https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/13/man-charged-with-plotting-attack-on-polish-pm/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 20:38:48 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105477

A 66-year-old Polish man has been charged with planning an attack on Prime Minister Donald Tusk as part of an attempt to overthrow the government. A search of his home revealed improvised explosive devices that he allegedly planned to use in the plot.

The suspect, who can be named only as Krzysztof N. under Polish privacy law, has also been charged with a number of other offences, including promoting a war of aggression in Ukraine and inciting hate crimes. Media reports have identified the man as a radical-right extremist.

Do Prokuratury Okręgowej w Warszawie został doprowadzony 66-letni Krzysztof N., zatrzymany w związku z planowaniem zamachu na @donaldtusk i @KosiniakKamysz ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/rjcR3rNvyW

— tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 13, 2026

On Sunday, Poland’s security services announced that they had received what they described as “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Tusk and his defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz.

Later that day, a 66-year-old suspect was detained in the city of Wrocław, southwest Poland, and his property was searched. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński told broadcaster TVP that the man was “very active in groups promoting extreme views”.

On Tuesday, the district prosecutor’s office in Warsaw, where Krzysztof N. has been transported, announced that he had been charged with nine offences.

“The most serious charge is for planning to forcibly overthrow state authorities, including the prime minister and cabinet, using explosives,” said spokesman Piotr Antoni Skiba. That crime carries a potential prison sentence of up to 15 years.

 

Skiba revealed that “a dozen or so” improvised explosive devices, which appeared to be similar to fragmentation grenades, had been found in the man’s home. There was also a crossbow, sharp-tipped metal bolts, and what are believed to be blank-firing or pneumatic guns.

Skiba said that Krzysztof N.’s plans had been discovered after an anonymous person sent a message to the State Protection Service (SOP), which is responsible for the security of high-ranking officials, that included a recording of a conversation purportedly with the suspect.

Krzysztof N. could be heard claiming that he had gathered “sevel hundred people” who shared his ideological beliefs and would help him overthrown the Polish government by force.

At the moment, there is no indication that Krzysztof N. or the group around him were inspired in any way by foreign intelligence agencies, but the issue is still being investigated, added Skiba, quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP).

Poland’s security services say they have received “credible” information indicating a “high probability” of an assassination attempt against Prime Minister Donald Tusk and defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz https://t.co/zl3vt6mah3

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 11, 2026

Among the other charges Krzysztof N. has heard are “promoting a war of aggression, including in Ukraine, as well as incitement to commit crimes based on nationality, ethnicity, race and political views”, added Skiba. The suspect has so far pleaded not guilty on all counts.

On Monday, Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading daily, reported that Krzysztof N. had for months been posting videos online calling on fellow right-wing extremists to fight against the authorities. He also expressed antisemitic and anti-Ukrainian sentiment.

Another newspaper, Rzeczpospolita, found that he runs a Facebook page called Radical Polish Resistance Movement that has almost 8,000 followers and claims Poland’s two main political parties – Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) – are “in the hands of globalists and Judeo-communists”.

"Patriota do przesady". Kim jest Krzysztof N., Wrocławianin podejrzewany przez służby o planowanie zamachu na premiera Tuska

Mężczyzna, który miał planować zamach na premiera Donalda Tuska Od kilku miesięcy nagrywał w mediach społecznościowych filmiki i skrzykiwał prawicowych…

— Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 12, 2026

In a separate case, government spokesman Adam Szłapka announced on Tuesday that a 46-year-old man in the town of Oborniki in western Poland had been detained on suspicion of publicly calling for the murder of Tusk and the speaker of parliament, Włodzimierz Czarzasty.

A spokeswoman for the district prosecutor’s office in Oborniki told PAP that the man had been charged with inciting murder, for which he could face up to three years in prison.

“He admitted to publishing content insulting various government officials, but denied the charge of inciting their murder,” she revealed. “He expressed regret and remorse.”

]]> Poland and Norway sign declaration on deepening security ties https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/13/poland-and-norway-sign-declaration-on-deepening-security-ties/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 14:31:19 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105448

Poland and Norway have signed a declaration on deepening security cooperation, including joint defence production, strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks, and continuing to support Ukraine.

“In a world where the international order, laws and principles are being violated by the world’s biggest players, Poland and Norway show how partnership can be built on shared values and interests,” said Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, alongside his Norwegian counterpart, Jonas Gahr Støre.

🇵🇱🤝🇳🇴 Strategiczne partnerstwo Polski i Królestwa Norwegii oficjalnie przypieczętowane.

✍️ Podpisano deklarację o strategicznym partnerstwie między obu państwami, stanowiącą efekt wieloletniej współpracy oraz wspólnoty interesów biznesowych, geopolitycznych i moralnych.

🛡️ W… pic.twitter.com/vBrWrdC8oT

— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 12, 2026

The two leaders signed a declaration on strategic partnership during a visit by a Norwegian delegation to the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year’s partner country. The agreement sets out a framework for closer long-term cooperation between the two countries.

Among the commitments made by the two countries are “deeper operational cooperation” and expanding joint procurement and production between their respective defence industries.

Warsaw and Oslo also pledged to work together on strengthening NATO’s eastern and northern flanks, as well as to coordinate responses to cyberattacks, hybrid operations and foreign information manipulation.

“The point is that Europe should take on greater responsibility for security,” said Støre. “We must invest in it more coherently and consistently, so as to avoid duplication, but invest in such a way that regional defence systems are stronger.”

 

The declaration also promises continued support for Ukraine in its defence against Russia, as well as efforts to ensure a just and lasting peace and to “hold Russia accountable for its war of aggression”.

Although security issues dominate the declaration, the two countries also pledged to deepen economic ties, including in the energy and maritime sectors.

Robin Allers, a scholar at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that the move to sign the declaration with Poland was part of a broader Norwegian strategy to deepen mutual commitments with key NATO partners amid uncertainty over US engagement in Europe.

“Today’s agreement demonstrates your country’s increasingly important role in Europe,” said Allers, pointing to Poland’s growing economic and military strength, as well as its role in supporting Ukraine.

Poland has unveiled its first frigate to enter service in decades at a ceremony in the Baltic port of Gdynia, where the ship was constructed.

It will be followed by two more new frigates as part of a €3.5bn programme to modernise the ageing Polish fleet https://t.co/093Fx2WSM7

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026

Poland has in recent years also moved to strengthen its ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. This year, Polish and Norwegian companies announced plans to develop a new anti-drone system for Poland in the wake of incursions of Russian drones into Polish airspace.

Last year, Norway opened a facility in Poland, Camp Jomsborg, for training Ukrainian military personnel. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland.

The two countries also have close energy ties. In 2022, the Baltic Pipe began delivering Norwegian gas to Poland, helping the country reduce its reliance on Russian supplies. Norway’s Equinor is also involved in developing one of Poland’s first offshore wind farms in the Baltic.

Poland will manufacture the missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is buying from South Korea.

The Norwegian government says that Polish production "will strengthen security of supply for Norway and other European customers of the system" https://t.co/NIJj7owK45

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 29, 2026

Poland has also moved closer in recent years to Sweden, with which it signed a strategic partnership in 2024. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab.

Last year, at Poland’s suggestion, NATO launched a new military mission to protect critical infrastructure in the Baltic Sea.

On Monday this week, Norway’s defence ministry announced that Poland will join an initiative recently launched by 11 European countries and Canada to cooperate more closely on security in the North Atlantic, Arctic and Baltic Sea.

]]> Germany detains Turks suspected of sabotaging Starlink station in Poland on behalf of Russia https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/13/germany-detains-turks-suspected-of-sabotaging-starlink-station-in-poland-on-behalf-of-russia/ Tue, 13 Oct 2026 09:04:55 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105435

Two Turkish men suspected of carrying out last month’s arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink have been detained in Germany. The Polish authorities say that the sabotage was carried out on behalf of Russia.

On Monday evening, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk first announced that the pair had been taken into custody “at the request of the Polish security services”.

He said that the Turkish men’s actions had been “a further act of hybrid warfare” – the term used for sabotage and other hostile activity carried out in Europe by Russia – and that “the perpetrators will answer before the Polish justice system”.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that the case is “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history since the fall of communism”, and that it is “beyond any doubt” that the Israeli firm behind Pegasus, NSO Group, cooperates with Israeli intelligence.

Pegasus is a powerful and controversial tool that allows the extraction of large amounts of data from mobile phones without users’ knowledge. A number of countries have been found to have used it to spy on opposition figures.

In 2017, Poland, under the government of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, purchased Pegasus from NSO. The spyware was subsequently used against hundreds of targets, including a number of PiS’s political opponents.

Among them was the head of the 2019 election campaign of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party (which was then known as Civic Platform, PO). Last year, Tusk revealed that his own wife and daughter had been among those caught up in the surveillance.

PiS, however, has insisted that Pegasus was a necessary tool to fight crime and ensure national security. It says the spyware was only used with court approval against targets legitimately suspected of wrongdoing.

 

After a coalition led by Tusk took power from PiS in December 2023, it launched investigations into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Today, the National Prosecutor’s Office released its latest findings, based on analysis by experts at the forensic research office of Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW).

The experts confirmed that Pegasus allowed the harvesting of emails, instant messaging and text messages; the content of telephone conversations, both via mobile networks and internet calls; browsing histories, calendars and contact lists; photos, videos and other files; and location data.

“Additionally, Pegasus allowed the use of the device’s built-in microphone and cameras to record audio and video in real time and take screenshots,” reports the National Prosecutor’s Office.

The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar.

After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time.

The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF

 

A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”.

Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska.

Patrick Lewis, who sits on the board of London-listed Sanderson Design Group, warned the boss of LBV Asset Management against “potentially defamatory allegations” after he questioned the pay packets [...]]]>

A board member of the under-fire interior designer favoured by the King threatened to sue the founder of its biggest shareholder in a tussle over pay.

Patrick Lewis, who sits on the board of London-listed Sanderson Design Group, warned the boss of LBV Asset Management against “potentially defamatory allegations” after he questioned the pay packets of the company’s executives. 

LBV has been pushing to remove former National Lottery boss Dame Dianne Thompson, Sanderson’s chairwoman, over the design group’s drift towards “inaction and inertia”. 

Sanderson Design Group holds a Royal Warrant and strong ties to King Charles III, and traces its history back to the arts and craft movement pioneer William Morris. 

LBV, which owns 14 per cent of the design group’s shares, has sought to put the spotlight on the pay packets handed to the group’s executives following “years of poor performance”. 

The group’s chief executive and finance chief, Lisa Montague and Mike Woodcock, were handed a combined pay packet worth £1.13m last year, equivalent to 36 per cent of the company’s pre-tax profit. 

In a letter to Sanderson’s board, LBV said the 26 per cent shareholder vote against the firm’s remuneration report at its annual meeting was “clear evidence of dissatisfaction among shareholders when it comes to board and executive compensation”.

Shareholder ‘baffled’ by threat

Patrick Lewis, who is an independent non-executive director and chair of Sanderson’s remuneration committee, wrote back to Emmanuel de Figueiredo, LBV’s founder, to warn him “the allegations contained in your letter have the potential to cause serious damage” to the group’s executives. 

In the letter, seen by City AM, he wrote: “My strong recommendation would be that you should not take any further steps to publish, circulate or repeat the allegations contained in your letter in their current form. 

“I expressly reserve all of our rights and remedies available to us, including the right to seek legal advice and pursue such action as may be appropriate in respect of any defamatory statements that are published. 

“I nevertheless hope that this will not be necessary and that any concerns raised by LBV can be addressed through proper and constructive engagement rather than through the publication of misleading and potentially defamatory allegations.”

Lewis has been a director at Sanderson since November 2021. Before joining the design group he served as finance chief of department store giant John Lewis, which he first joined in 1994.

‘They see us as troublemakers’

In LBV’s response to Lewis’s letter, de Figueiredo said it was “baffling” that he had interpreted his comments about Montague and Woodcock’s pay as “attacks on the executive management team”.

In the correspondence, the hedge fund boss wrote: “We categorically reject the characterisation in your letter that our comments amount, expressly or by implication, to an allegation that either executive is unsuitable for office and, therefore, defamatory or misleading in any way.”

LBV addressed Lewis’s threat in a circular sent to shareholders on Tuesday, saying: “A board that meets those legitimate views with the threat of legal action appears to believe its shareholders should not hold views of their own. They see us as troublemakers, rather than as stakeholders to be taken seriously.”

Sanderson’s investors have been called to an emergency meeting on 29 October to vote on LBV’s proposals to remove Dame Thompson and elect Stephen Brook as a director.

“LBV’s proposals risk significant disruption and uncertainty at precisely the point when the benefits of the group’s transformation are becoming increasingly evident,” Thompson has said to shareholders.

Sanderson Design Group and Lewis declined to comment.

Shares in storage firm Big Yellow bounced on Wednesday after an activist investor urged the company to put itself up for sale.  The FTSE 250 self-storage provider jumped more than five per cent to 844p after Ancora Alternatives, which owns four per cent of the group, told it to consider a take-private deal. Shares in storage firm Big Yellow bounced on Wednesday after an activist investor urged the company to put itself up for sale. 

The FTSE 250 self-storage provider jumped more than five per cent to 844p after Ancora Alternatives, which owns four per cent of the group, told it to consider a take-private deal.

The Ohio-based investment firm told shareholders that Big Yellow, the UK’s largest self-storage provider, is “full of trapped value”. 

The storage group is trading at a 39 per cent discount to the value of its assets, the investor said, despite having a “highly resilient business model”. 

Big Yellow offers storage across 113 sites in the UK, with its property estate concentrated around prime, main-road locations in London and the South East. 

Ancora said a sale of the London-listed firm would be the “best risk-adjusted outcome for shareholders,” adding that there are a number of potential buyers who would snap up Big Yellow’s “premium London-based portfolio”. 

The storage firm offers a more attractive asset to potential buyers than its US rivals because it would come at a cheaper price and offers rare access to high-value London properties, Ancora argued.

Big Yellow axes Blackstone talks

Big Yellow held sales talks with Blackstone last year but terminated discussions after the asset manager submitted an offer. Any deal for Big Yellow would come amid a wave of takeovers of UK property firms, whose valuable portfolios and sluggish share prices have made them a draw to private equity buyers.

Blackstone took control of Warehouse REIT for £489m in September last year, and FTSE 100 property investor Segro agreed to a £14bn takeover by US rival Prologis in August this year.

Big Yellow is currently suffering from “rising UK interest rates, sluggish GDP growth and a weak housing market,” which have stifled demand for domestic storage because Brits are moving home less often, Ancora said.

But the investor said the storage firm is well poised to benefit from “the possibility of an improved macroeconomic environment” in the UK and London. 

“If the Company were to run a strategic review and solicit interest from all available parties, a transaction would likely occur at a valuation above Blackstone’s,” Ancora said.

Analysts at stock broker Peel Hunt said: “It is hard to argue against the quality of the business, and its portfolio.”

They added that the group’s share price “currently undervalues this quality and its medium-term prospects” but questioned whether a sale would “adequately” boost shareholder value. 

Surrey-based Big Yellow was founded in 1998 and delivered a two per cent uplift in revenue to £209m in the year to March. Its profit before tax slipped by 38 per cent to £126m.

Big Yellow was declined to comment.

]]> 2465652Felix Armstrong Felix Armstrong UK state growing at faster pace than France after spending splurge and tax hikes https://www.cityam.com/uk-state-growing-at-faster-pace-than-france-after-spending-splurge-and-tax-hikes/ Wed, 14 Oct 2026 09:39:44 +0000 https://www.cityam.com/?p=2465648

The size of the British state is growing by a larger amount than any other G7 nation apart from Germany since the pandemic in 2020, figures on government spending from the International Monetary Fund have shown.  The IMF’s latest report on countries’ fiscal outlook shows that UK government spending is set to rise by 5.2 [...]]]>

The size of the British state is growing by a larger amount than any other G7 nation apart from Germany since the pandemic in 2020, figures on government spending from the International Monetary Fund have shown. 

The IMF’s latest report on countries’ fiscal outlook shows that UK government spending is set to rise by 5.2 percentage points between 2019 and 2031. 

This will make the size of the state rise to 43.3 per cent of GDP in 2030 compared to a level of just 38.1 per cent before Covid-19 dramatically changed the course of public finances. 

The US, France, Italy, Canada and Japan are projected to increase government spending by a smaller proportion as a share of their economies. France, Italy and Canada already spend more as a share of GDP. 

Germany is the only country among the seven dominant economies that is set to increase spending by a higher level. Chancellor Friedrich Merz announced last year that borrowing rules would be significantly loosened to fund 838 billion euros (more than £700bn) in mainly defence investment through to 2030. 

The fund’s report adds to anticipation ahead of Chancellor John Healey’s first budget, where he will be required to juggle spending pressures for the cost of living with limited scope against a difficult fiscal outlook.

Higher spending funded by huge tax rises

IMF forecasts also continued to project that the tax burden in the UK would grow at the fastest pace among advanced economies. 

Revenue as a share of GDP will come to about 41.9 per cent by 2031 following tax raids on businesses and households by the Labour government, rising from 38.2 per cent in 2025. 

Under current government plans, this would mean that the UK would go from having the second largest deficit in the G7, after only the US, in 2025 to posting the smallest one by 2031 at -1.4 per cent of GDP. 

IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva praised Labour ministers for taking “decisive” measures to limit borrowing as she said she thinks “the government recognises they need to stay the course”. On Wednesday, it was reported in the Financial Times that Chancellor John Healey would not raise borrowing in order to fund cost of living or business support, instead using tax hikes or spending cuts to fund proposals. 

However, IMF officials warned the Chancellor against raising the tax burden further to fund defence spending. 

Rodrigo Valdés, who leads the IMF’s research on fiscal policy, called for an “urgent” discussion about spending cuts when he was asked about how the UK could spend more on the military. 

“In general, Europe has relatively high revenue ratios. So the space for a lot more revenues is not easy,” he said. 

“[Tax] distorts at the end of the day, so the discussion about the social contract behind spending is very, very urgent in the sense that… less spending [will be] part of the new pressures that you will have from different sources.”

He added: “Debt spending will be very persistent. Defence spending will be persistent. So, even if you accommodate temporary risk with debt, you have to be prepared at some point to recognise that debt cannot forever finance this part.”

Should Andy Burnham call a snap election? Emily Sheffield reports from the political tittle tattle field of David Cameron’s 60th party in today’s Notebook

Party chat turns to politics at David Cameron’s 60th

This weekend in Cornwall, celebrating David Cameron’s 60th birthday, politics was refreshingly off the menu. This was all about family and old friends, cold water plunges, wind-blown hikes to shed hangovers and a lot of eating. Only once did talk briefly slip onto Westminster’s current obsession: will Andy Burnham hold a snap election.

The verdict from the politicos present was split. Most pinned spring 2027 as the likeliest date, not December; 2028 a strong possibility and 2029 the least likely. But everyone agreed that for Burnham the risks could still outweigh the gains, even if his advisors persuade him differently.

Firstly, what is his reason for the voting public about why he’s going to the polls? This was Theresa May’s mistake. She had none, then lost the sizable majority won by Cameron and never really recovered. Whereas Boris Johnson had a clear argument: Get Brexit Done. The polls point to Burnham being still short of a majority and losing 99 seats.

True, their ‘Lean Left’ strategy is working, so they could soon hit 30 per cent. But the public want PMs to get on with the job, polling can change fast in a fevered run-up.
